profiles.name: Tropical aroid

watering.how: Water slowly over the whole soil until it runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer after a few minutes. Never leave the pot standing in water.
watering.growing: Water when the top 3 cm of soil feel dry to your finger.
watering.dormant: Let the top half of the soil dry before watering. Growth slows and the roots rot easily in cold, wet soil.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil, never on dry roots.
fertilizer.dormant: Stop feeding. The plant can't use it, and the salts build up in the soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east window, or a metre or two back from a south or west one. Morning sun is fine; hot midday sun scorches the leaves. It likes warmth (above 15 °C) and more humidity than most homes have, so keep it away from radiators and cold draughts.

profiles.soil: A chunky, airy mix: about half houseplant compost with bark and perlite. Roots need air as much as water.

profiles.name: Succulent

watering.how: Soak the soil until water runs from the drainage holes, then let it drain completely. Water the soil, not the rosette: water sitting in the leaves rots them.
watering.growing: Water only when the soil is dry all the way down. Push a wooden skewer to the bottom: if it comes out clean, water.
watering.dormant: Water very little, just enough to stop the leaves from wrinkling. Cold, wet soil is what kills succulents in winter.

fertilizer.type: Cactus and succulent fertiliser, low in nitrogen (roughly 1-2-2)
fertilizer.growing: Feed at a quarter to half the strength on the label, a few times across the Growing season, on moist soil.

light.text: As much light as you can give: a south or west window, with direct sun. Move a plant from shade into full sun gradually, or it burns. Dry air suits it, and a cool winter spot (about 10 °C) suits it, but never frost.

profiles.soil: Gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, or houseplant compost with at least a third of pumice or perlite. Use a pot with a drainage hole, terracotta if you tend to overwater.

profiles.name: Calathea and prayer plant

watering.how: Water with rain or filtered water, or tap water left to stand overnight, until it runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer. Hard tap water browns the leaf edges.
watering.growing: Keep the soil evenly moist, never soggy: water as soon as the surface feels dry.
watering.dormant: Let the top 2 cm of soil dry before watering, but never let the whole pot dry out.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Medium, indirect light: a north or east window, or well back from a south or west one. Direct sun fades the patterns and scorches the leaves. It needs warmth (above 16 °C) and high humidity: a bathroom with a window, a humidifier, or a group of plants.

profiles.soil: A moisture-holding but airy mix: peat-free houseplant compost with some perlite and bark.

profiles.name: Fern

watering.how: Water until it runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer. Rain or filtered water is best. Never let the root ball dry out completely.
watering.growing: Keep the soil evenly moist: water as soon as the surface starts to feel dry.
watering.dormant: Water a little less, letting just the surface dry, but keep the root ball moist.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at a quarter to half the strength on the label: ferns are light feeders and their roots burn easily.

light.text: Medium to bright, indirect light: a north or east window, or a few metres back from a south or west one. Direct sun crisps the fronds. Most want more humidity than a heated room has, so a bright bathroom or kitchen suits them, away from radiators.

profiles.soil: A light, moisture-holding mix: peat-free houseplant compost with some bark or coir, and perlite for air.

profiles.name: Leafy tropical

watering.how: Water until it runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer after a few minutes.
watering.growing: Water when the top 2 cm of soil feel dry. Soft leaves wilt fast when the pot dries out, and most perk up within hours of a drink.
watering.dormant: Let a little more of the soil dry, about the top third, before watering.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east or west window, or a metre or two back from a south one. A little morning sun keeps coloured leaves bright; too little light makes them pale and leggy. Keep it above 15 °C and away from radiators and cold draughts.

profiles.soil: Peat-free houseplant compost with a handful of perlite for drainage. Pinch out the growing tips in the Growing season to keep it bushy.

profiles.name: Begonia

watering.how: Water the soil, never the leaves: wet leaves get mildew and spots. Water until it drains, then empty the saucer.
watering.growing: Water when the top 2 cm of soil feel dry. Begonias mind soggy soil far more than a little dryness.
watering.dormant: Let the top half of the soil dry before watering.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east window, or back from a south or west one. Morning sun is fine; hot sun burns the leaves. It likes warmth (above 15 °C) and humid air that still moves around the leaves, so don't mist it.

profiles.soil: A light, airy mix: peat-free houseplant compost with plenty of perlite, in a shallow pot that suits its fine roots.

profiles.name: African violet and relatives

watering.how: Water from below: stand the pot in room-temperature water for half an hour, then let it drain. Cold water on the leaves leaves pale marks.
watering.growing: Water when the top of the soil feels dry. Keep it lightly moist, never soggy.
watering.dormant: Water a little less, letting the top 2 cm dry. Most keep flowering in a warm, bright room.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at a quarter to half the strength on the label, on moist soil.
fertilizer.dormant: Feed at a quarter of the strength while it's flowering; otherwise stop.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east or north window, or back from a south or west one, out of direct sun, which scorches the leaves. With too little light it grows leaves but no flowers. It likes steady warmth (18 to 24 °C) and no draughts.

profiles.soil: A light, peat-free African violet mix, or houseplant compost with a third of perlite. Keep the pot small: it flowers best a little snug.

profiles.name: Indoor tree

watering.how: Water slowly over the whole soil until it drains from the holes, then empty the saucer. A big pot dries from the top down, so check deeper than the surface.
watering.growing: Water when the top 3 to 5 cm of soil feel dry.
watering.dormant: Let the top half of the soil dry before watering. Cold, wet roots are the usual reason an indoor tree drops its leaves in winter.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Bright light with a few hours of sun: close to an east or west window, or a metre or two back from a south one. Pick its spot and leave it there: most indoor trees drop leaves after a move. Keep it above 15 °C, away from radiators, draughts and doors.

profiles.soil: Peat-free houseplant compost with some bark and perlite, in a heavy pot that won't tip. Repot one size up only when the roots fill the pot.

profiles.name: Tough foliage

watering.how: Soak the soil until water runs from the drainage holes, then let it drain completely. Keep water out of the centre of the leaves.
watering.growing: Water only when the soil has dried almost to the bottom of the pot. Push a finger or a wooden skewer deep: if it's still damp, wait.
watering.dormant: Water very little: only when the soil is dry right through, and less still in a cool room. Far more of these die of water than of neglect.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label a couple of times across the Growing season.

light.text: Anywhere from a north window to a bright south one: it tolerates low light but grows faster in bright light, and takes a few hours of sun once used to it. Ordinary room temperatures and dry air suit it; keep it above 10 °C.

profiles.soil: A free-draining mix: houseplant compost with a third of perlite or grit, in a pot with a drainage hole. It likes a snug pot, so repot only when the roots crowd it.

profiles.name: Palm

watering.how: Water until it drains from the holes, then empty the saucer. Palms dislike hard tap water: rain or filtered water keeps the tips greener.
watering.growing: Water when the top 2 to 3 cm of soil feel dry. Keep it lightly moist, never soggy.
watering.dormant: Let the top half of the soil dry before watering.

fertilizer.type: Palm fertiliser, or a balanced one with magnesium (roughly 3-1-3)
fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east or west window, or a metre or two back from a south one. Most indoor palms burn in hot midday sun, and some cope with a shadier corner. Keep it above 13 °C, away from radiators, and raise the humidity if the tips brown.

profiles.soil: A free-draining mix: houseplant compost with bark and perlite. Palms like snug pots and hate root disturbance, so repot only when the roots lift the plant.

profiles.name: Orchid

watering.how: Water over the bark until it runs from the holes, or soak the pot in room-temperature water for a few minutes, then let it drain completely. Never leave water standing where the leaves meet.
watering.growing: Water when the bark feels dry and the roots look silvery; green roots still have water.
watering.dormant: Water less, letting the bark dry right through. Many orchids rest after flowering.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at a quarter to half the strength on the label, and flush the bark with plain water now and then.
fertilizer.dormant: Stop feeding, or feed at a quarter of the strength if it's still growing.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east window, or a metre back from a south or west one behind a sheer curtain. Mid-green leaves mean the light is right: dark green means too little, yellowish too much. Keep it above 15 °C; nights a few degrees cooler help it flower.

profiles.soil: Never soil: an orchid bark mix in a clear pot with holes, so air reaches the roots and you can see them. Repot into fresh bark after flowering once the old bark breaks down.

profiles.name: Bromeliad

watering.how: Water the soil lightly and keep a little water in the central cup, if it has one. Tip the cup out and refill it now and then so the water doesn't go stale. Rain or filtered water is best.
watering.growing: Let the top of the soil dry between waterings: the roots mostly anchor the plant.
watering.dormant: Keep the soil on the dry side, and the cup only a little wet, or empty in a cool room.

fertilizer.type: Balanced liquid fertiliser (roughly 1-1-1), or an orchid one
fertilizer.growing: Feed at a quarter of the strength on the label, on the soil or misted on the leaves.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east or west window, or back from a south one. Soft, green-leaved kinds burn in hot sun; stiff, grey ones take more. It likes warmth (above 15 °C) and humid air.

profiles.soil: A light, airy mix: orchid bark with some houseplant compost, in a small pot. The rosette slowly dies after flowering: pot up the pups that grow around it.

profiles.name: Air plant

watering.how: Soak the whole plant in rain or filtered water for 20 to 30 minutes, shake it out, and let it dry upside down within a few hours. Water trapped at the base rots it.
watering.growing: Soak it whenever the leaves feel less firm and look greyer, or start to curl. Mist it in between if the air is dry.
watering.dormant: Soak it less often and more briefly in a cool room, and dry it well.

fertilizer.growing: Now and then, add a quarter of the strength on the label to the soaking water.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: close to an east or west window, or back from a south one. Grey, fuzzy kinds take some direct sun; green, smooth ones prefer shade. Air must move around it, so never keep it in a closed glass container.

profiles.soil: No soil: set it on wood, stone or a stand, or in a shell or dish that doesn't hold water.

profiles.name: Hoya, peperomia and succulent vine

watering.how: Water until it drains from the holes, then empty the saucer. Thick leaves store water, so it forgives a dry spell far more than a wet one.
watering.growing: Water when the soil is dry for most of the pot's depth, or when the leaves feel a little softer when squeezed.
watering.dormant: Water sparingly: let the soil dry right through, then water lightly.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east or west window, or a metre back from a south one. A few hours of gentle sun keep it compact and help hoyas flower; deep shade makes it leggy. Keep it above 12 °C.

profiles.soil: An airy, fast-draining mix: houseplant compost with plenty of perlite and bark, in a small pot: the roots rot in a big one.

profiles.name: Desert cactus

watering.how: Soak the soil until water runs from the drainage holes, then let it drain completely. Water the soil, not the plant.
watering.growing: Water only when the soil is dry all the way down, then soak it.
watering.dormant: Keep it almost dry: water only if it starts to shrivel. A cool, dry rest is what makes most cacti flower.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at a quarter to half the strength on the label, a few times across the Growing season, on moist soil.

light.text: Full sun: the sunniest south or west window you have, or outdoors in summer. Bring it into strong sun gradually after a dim winter, or it scorches. A cool, bright winter spot (5 to 12 °C), out of frost, helps it flower.

profiles.soil: Gritty cactus mix, or houseplant compost with half pumice or grit, in a pot with a drainage hole. Hold it in a band of folded newspaper when you repot.

profiles.name: Forest cactus

watering.how: Water until it drains from the holes, then empty the saucer. Rain or filtered water suits it best.
watering.growing: Water when the top 2 cm of soil feel dry: it's a forest plant, not a desert one, and shouldn't dry out completely.
watering.dormant: Keep it cooler and drier, letting the top half of the soil dry. This rest sets the next flower buds.

fertilizer.type: Balanced liquid fertiliser (roughly 1-1-1), or a bloom one once buds form
fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label, on moist soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east or west window, or back from a south one. It grows on trees in the wild and scorches in hot midday sun. Once buds form, don't move or turn it, or they drop.

profiles.soil: A light, airy mix: houseplant compost with orchid bark and perlite. It flowers best a little pot-bound.

profiles.name: Carnivorous plant

watering.how: Use only rain, distilled or reverse-osmosis water: the minerals in tap water kill it. Stand the pot in a tray of it.
watering.growing: Keep the soil wet all the time: stand the pot in 1 to 2 cm of water and top up the tray once it's gone.
watering.dormant: Keep the soil moist but not standing in water. Most kinds from cool climates need a cold rest (below 10 °C), in an unheated bright room or outdoors.

fertilizer.growing: Don't feed it, and don't give it meat: the traps feed the plant, and fertiliser burns its roots.

light.text: Full sun: a south or west windowsill, or a sunny balcony in summer. Weak colour and floppy traps mean too little light.

profiles.soil: Nutrient-free: peat-free carnivorous plant mix, or sphagnum moss with perlite or lime-free horticultural sand. Never ordinary compost.

profiles.name: Tropical pitcher plant

watering.how: Use only rain, distilled or reverse-osmosis water: the minerals in tap water kill it. Water over the soil until it drains, and keep a little water in the pitchers.
watering.growing: Keep the soil moist but never standing in water: water as soon as the surface feels dry.
watering.dormant: Let the surface dry a little more between waterings. It needs no cold rest: keep it warm.

fertilizer.type: No fertiliser, or orchid fertiliser (roughly 1-1-1) at a quarter strength
fertilizer.growing: It feeds itself through its pitchers. If it grows no new pitchers, drop a pinch of quarter-strength orchid fertiliser into one or two of them, never onto the soil.

light.text: Bright, indirect light: an east window, or a metre back from a south or west one. Morning sun is fine; hot midday sun burns it. It needs warmth (above 15 °C) and humid air, or it stops making pitchers.

profiles.soil: Nutrient-free and airy: sphagnum moss with perlite and orchid bark, in a hanging pot so the pitchers can dangle. Never ordinary compost.

profiles.name: Mediterranean herb

watering.how: Water the soil until it drains, then let it drain fully. Never leave the pot standing in water.
watering.growing: Water when the top half of the soil is dry. Pots in full sun dry fast, so check them in hot weather.
watering.dormant: Water only when the soil is nearly dry right through. Wet roots in winter kill these more often than cold does.

fertilizer.growing: Feed lightly, at a quarter to half the strength on the label, a few times across the Growing season. Rich soil makes them soft and less fragrant.

light.text: Full sun: a south- or west-facing balcony, or the sunniest window indoors, with six hours of sun or more. In shade it grows leggy and loses its flavour. Most take a light frost outdoors in a free-draining pot, but not cold, soggy roots.

profiles.soil: Poor, gritty and free-draining: half compost, half grit or perlite, in a terracotta pot with a drainage hole. Cut it back after flowering to keep it bushy, but never into bare old wood.

profiles.name: Leafy herb

watering.how: Water the soil, not the leaves, until it drains. A supermarket pot is a crowd of seedlings: split it into a few pots so each clump gets water and light.
watering.growing: Keep the soil evenly moist: water as soon as the surface feels dry. Pots in sun dry fast in hot weather.
watering.dormant: Water less, letting the surface dry. Many die back or run to seed in the cold; tender ones like basil need a warm, bright windowsill indoors.

fertilizer.type: Balanced liquid fertiliser (roughly 1-1-1), organic if you eat the leaves
fertilizer.growing: Feed lightly, at half the strength on the label: too much makes big leaves with little flavour.

light.text: At least a few hours of sun: a south, east or west window, or a balcony with four to six hours of sun. Parsley, mint and chives cope with part shade; basil wants all the warmth and sun it can get.

profiles.soil: Peat-free multipurpose or vegetable compost with some perlite. Pick from the top and pinch out flower buds to keep the leaves coming.

profiles.name: Balcony shrub and climber

watering.how: Water slowly over the whole pot until it drains from the holes. A pot in full sun and wind dries out far faster than the ground.
watering.growing: Water when the top 3 to 5 cm of soil feel dry, and check often in hot weather.
watering.dormant: Water only when the soil is dry a good way down. Outdoors, rain may be enough; indoors in a cool, bright room, water sparingly.

fertilizer.type: Balanced liquid fertiliser (roughly 1-1-1), or a high-potash one (roughly 1-1-2) for flowering kinds
fertilizer.growing: Feed at the strength on the label, on moist soil.
fertilizer.dormant: Stop feeding, so new growth can toughen up before the cold.

light.text: Full sun: a south- or west-facing balcony or terrace, with six hours of sun or more. Hardiness varies: some take frost, and tender ones spend the winter indoors in a cool, bright room (5 to 12 °C).

profiles.soil: Loam-based or peat-free multipurpose compost with grit for weight and drainage, in a large pot with holes. Top-dress with fresh compost in spring, and repot when the roots fill the pot.

profiles.name: Citrus

watering.how: Water slowly until it drains, then empty the saucer. Rain water suits it: the lime in hard tap water yellows the leaves.
watering.growing: Water when the top 3 cm of soil feel dry, then soak it. Don't let it dry out while it's flowering or setting fruit.
watering.dormant: Let the top half of the soil dry before watering. A cool, bright spot (5 to 12 °C) suits it better than a warm, dark room.

fertilizer.type: Citrus fertiliser with iron and magnesium (roughly 3-1-2)
fertilizer.growing: Feed at the strength on the label, on moist soil.
fertilizer.dormant: Stop feeding, or feed at half the strength if it's kept warm and still growing.

light.text: Full sun: a south-facing balcony from late spring to autumn, and in winter a south or west window in the brightest, coolest room, out of frost. Move it between them gradually: a sudden change of light drops leaves.

profiles.soil: Free-draining citrus compost, or loam-based compost with a third of grit, lime-free, in a pot with holes.

profiles.name: Acid-loving shrub

watering.how: Use rain water: the lime in hard tap water yellows the leaves. Water until it drains, then empty the saucer.
watering.growing: Keep the soil evenly moist, never dry: water as soon as the surface feels dry, more in warm weather and while it's flowering.
watering.dormant: Water when the top 2 cm of soil are dry, and don't let the root ball dry out while buds are forming.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at the strength on the label, on moist soil, from the end of flowering through the Growing season.

light.text: Bright light with morning sun and shade at midday: an east window indoors, or an east- or north-facing balcony. Most like it cool; indoors, a hot, dry room makes them drop their buds.

profiles.soil: Ericaceous (lime-free) compost, peat-free, with some bark. Never ordinary multipurpose compost or garden lime.

profiles.name: Balcony flower and vegetable

watering.how: Water the soil, not the flowers or leaves, until it drains from the holes. Pots and window boxes in sun dry out fast: in a heatwave, check them morning and evening.
watering.growing: Keep the soil evenly moist: water as soon as the top feels dry. Never let it dry out completely, especially while flowering or fruiting.
watering.dormant: Many are grown for one season and finish with the cold. Ones kept over winter want a cool, bright spot and just enough water to stop the soil drying out.

fertilizer.type: High-potash liquid feed, such as tomato feed (roughly 1-1-3)
fertilizer.growing: Feed at the strength on the label from the first flowers on: potash keeps the flowers and fruit coming.

light.text: Full sun: a south- or west-facing balcony, with six hours of sun or more. Tender plants go out only after the last frost.

profiles.soil: Peat-free multipurpose compost with some perlite, in pots and boxes with drainage holes. Remove faded flowers to keep new ones coming.

profiles.name: Bulb and tuber

watering.how: Water the soil around the leaves, never onto the bulb itself, until it drains. Empty the saucer: a bulb in wet soil rots.
watering.growing: While it's in leaf and flowering, water when the top 2 cm of soil feel dry.
watering.dormant: Once flowering ends and the leaves yellow, water less, and stop once they've died back. Keep the resting bulb dry and cool until new shoots appear, then start again.

fertilizer.growing: Feed at half the strength on the label from the first flowers until the leaves start to yellow: this refills the bulb for next time.

light.text: Bright light with a few hours of sun: a south, east or west window, or a south- or west-facing balcony. Indoors, a cool room makes the flowers last longer.

profiles.soil: Free-draining compost with grit, in a pot with holes, each bulb planted about two to three times its own depth.

underwatering.name: Underwatering
underwatering.tell: The soil is dry and light all the way down, and the pot feels light when you lift it. Leaves are limp or crisp rather than soft.
underwatering.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains. If the soil has shrunk from the pot's sides, stand the pot in water for half an hour so it soaks up again.

overwatering.name: Overwatering
overwatering.tell: The soil is still damp days after watering, may smell sour, and yellowing starts low on the plant.
overwatering.fix: Let the soil dry further before watering again, empty the saucer, and check that the pot drains. A pot without a hole needs a plastic pot inside it.

root-rot.name: Root rot
root-rot.tell: Tip the plant out: healthy roots are firm and pale, rotten ones brown, soft and smelly. Stems may go soft at the base.
root-rot.fix: Cut away every soft root with clean scissors, repot into fresh, drier mix and a pot that drains, and water sparingly until new growth shows.

low-humidity.name: Dry air
low-humidity.tell: Only the tips and edges turn brown and papery, often near a radiator or air conditioning, while the soil moisture is right.
low-humidity.fix: Move it away from heat sources, group plants together, or stand the pot on a tray of wet pebbles. Misting does little.

salts.name: Fertiliser or tap-water salts
salts.tell: A white crust on the soil or the pot's rim, and tips browning even though watering is right.
salts.fix: Flush the soil: run plenty of water through it and let it drain. Feed at half strength, and use rain or filtered water if your tap water is hard.

age.name: Normal ageing
age.tell: One old leaf at the bottom at a time turns yellow, while new leaves come in healthy.
age.fix: Nothing to fix. Remove the leaf once it's fully yellow.

low-light.name: Too little light
low-light.tell: New growth is pale, small and stretched, with long gaps between leaves, and the plant leans toward the window.
low-light.fix: Move it closer to a window, and turn the pot a quarter each time you water so it grows evenly. Stretched growth won't shorten, but new growth will be compact.

sunburn.name: Sunburn
sunburn.tell: Bleached, beige or brown patches on the side facing the window, appearing after a move or a sunny spell.
sunburn.fix: Shade it with a sheer curtain or move it back, then bring it into sun gradually. Burnt patches stay; new growth will be fine.

leaf-spot.name: Leaf spot
leaf-spot.tell: Brown or black spots with a yellow ring around them, spreading, usually after water sat on the leaves.
leaf-spot.fix: Remove the spotted leaves, water the soil rather than the leaves, and give the plant more air around it.

cold.name: Cold or draughts
cold.tell: Leaves drop or darken suddenly after a cold night, an open window or a move next to a door.
cold.fix: Move it somewhere steadily warm and away from doors and windows that open. Damaged leaves won't recover.

moved.name: A recent move
moved.tell: Leaves drop soon after it came home or changed spot, and nothing else is wrong.
moved.fix: Leave it in its new spot and keep watering as usual. Most plants settle in on their own.

rootbound.name: Outgrown pot
rootbound.tell: Roots circle the pot or grow out of the drainage holes, and water runs straight through.
rootbound.fix: Repot one size up in the Growing season.

dormancy.name: Dormant season
dormancy.tell: It's the Dormant season and the plant is otherwise healthy.
dormancy.fix: Nothing to fix. Growth resumes when the Growing season starts.

spider-mites.name: Spider mites
spider-mites.tell: Fine pale speckles on the leaves and thin webbing under them and where leaves meet stems. Wipe a leaf's underside with white tissue: tiny moving specks are mites.
spider-mites.fix: Shower the plant, undersides too, then wipe or spray the leaves with insecticidal soap every few days until no mites are left. Mites love dry air, so raise the humidity.

mealybugs.name: Mealybugs
mealybugs.tell: White, cottony tufts in leaf joints and under leaves, sometimes with sticky residue.
mealybugs.fix: Dab each tuft with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then treat with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating until none come back. Keep the plant apart from the others meanwhile.

scale.name: Scale insects
scale.tell: Small brown or tan bumps on stems and leaf veins that scrape off with a fingernail, and sticky leaves below them.
scale.fix: Scrape them off with a fingernail or a cotton bud with rubbing alcohol, then wipe with neem oil or insecticidal soap, repeating until no new bumps appear.

fungus-gnats.name: Fungus gnats
fungus-gnats.tell: Tiny black flies that rise from the soil when you water. They're a nuisance; their larvae in wet soil can nibble roots.
fungus-gnats.fix: Let the top of the soil dry out more between waterings, set yellow sticky traps, and water from the bottom for a while.

thrips.name: Thrips
thrips.tell: Silvery streaks and tiny black dots on the leaves, and slender insects that dart away when you shake a leaf over white paper.
thrips.fix: Shower the plant, set blue or yellow sticky traps, and spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil until the streaks stop spreading.

mildew.name: Powdery mildew
mildew.tell: A white, dusty coating on the leaves that wipes off with a finger, often in still, humid air or on a plant whose roots are dry.
mildew.fix: Remove the worst leaves, water the soil rather than the leaves, and give the plant more air and light. Keep it from drying out at the roots.

no-rest.name: No rest
no-rest.tell: It grew all winter in a warm room and has never set buds, though it has enough light.
no-rest.fix: Give it a cooler, drier rest in the Dormant season, in a bright spot: that rest is what sets the buds.

nitrogen.name: Too much nitrogen
nitrogen.tell: Plenty of lush leaves but few or no flowers, after feeding with a general or leafy-plant fertiliser.
nitrogen.fix: Switch to a high-potash or flowering fertiliser at the strength on the label, and give it more sun.

hunger.name: Hungry soil
hunger.tell: Older leaves turn pale yellow all over, and new growth is small and slow, in old compost that has had little feeding.
hunger.fix: Feed at the strength on the label through the Growing season, and repot into fresh compost if the old one has broken down.

hard-water.name: Lime in hard water
hard-water.tell: New leaves turn yellow while their veins stay green, on a plant that likes acid soil or gets hard tap water.
hard-water.fix: Water with rain or filtered water, feed with a fertiliser for acid-loving plants that has iron in it, and repot into lime-free compost if it doesn't improve.

aphids.name: Aphids
aphids.tell: Clusters of small green, black or grey insects on shoot tips and flower buds, with sticky leaves below them.
aphids.fix: Rub them off with your fingers or wash them off with a jet of water, then spray with insecticidal soap until no more appear. On a balcony, ladybirds eat them.

whitefly.name: Whitefly
whitefly.tell: Tiny white insects that fly up in a cloud when you touch the plant, with sticky leaves below.
whitefly.fix: Hang yellow sticky traps, wash the undersides of the leaves, and spray with insecticidal soap until the cloud is gone.

symptoms.name: Brown spots with a yellow ring
Tiny white flies on the leaves

Q149401.funFact: The miniature form sold as fairy castle cactus gets its name from curving branches that look like castle turrets. The wild species is a tall cactus whose white flowers open around midnight and close by dawn, visited by hummingbird moths.

Q311994.careNotes: It drops its leaves and rests in winter: keep it dry and above 10 °C until new leaves appear.
Q311994.funFact: The fat, swollen base is a water-storing caudex. On the island of Socotra, one form of the plant can build a base 2.4 m across.

Q4678994.careNotes: Maidenhair ferns never forgive drying out: keep the soil moist at all times and the air humid.
Q4678994.funFact: Botanists were surprised in 2020 to find it thriving in the 14th-century tunnels under Znojmo in the Czech Republic, kept going by the damp air and the lights put in for tourist tours.

Q2797160.careNotes: Maidenhair ferns never forgive drying out: keep the soil moist at all times and the air humid.
Q2797160.funFact: Its genus name comes from the Greek adiantos, meaning 'unwetted', a reference to the leaves. The maidenhair part comes from the glossy dark leaf stalks, which look like human hair.

Q4685810.funFact: Besides crinkle leaf plant, it also goes by Key Lime Pie. Its short upright stems are wrapped in a fuzz of fine aerial roots, and it grows wild only in the Eastern Cape of South Africa.

Q974721.funFact: In the wild, the water pooled in its leaf funnels can hold tiny ecosystems of small animals, algae and even aquatic plants. Its flowers open blue, then turn red at the tips as they fade.

Q138279.careNotes: It grows from autumn to spring and rests in summer heat, when the rosettes close up. Water less in summer, not in winter.
Q138279.funFact: Despite the nickname Irish rose, it grows wild only in the western Canary Islands, on Tenerife, La Palma, El Hierro, La Gomera and Gran Canaria. Plants found along Mediterranean and Moroccan coasts are thought to be later arrivals.

Q511569.careNotes: It grows from autumn to spring and rests in summer heat, when the rosettes close up. Water less in summer, not in winter.
Q511569.funFact: In the wild it is a beach plant that lives in sand on the Canary Islands and in northern Africa, and it has since made itself at home in similar climates such as Southern California.

Q4688539.careNotes: It likes to dry a little more between waterings than an African violet, and can be watered from the top.
Q4688539.funFact: The name lipstick plant comes from its scarlet flowers, which push out of buds that look like tubes of lipstick. In the wild it grows perched on trees or rocks in the humid tropics, from the Malay Peninsula to Java.

Q161246.careNotes: Evergreen kinds keep their leaves in winter: water them lightly then, in a frost-free spot. It flowers best crowded in its pot.
Q161246.funFact: Its roots are strong enough to crack concrete, and one plant can live for up to 75 years. Most agapanthus in gardens are hybrids or cultivars of this single South African species.

Q1254225.funFact: Most agaves send up a straight, towering flower spike, but this one's arches over and droops back down, which is where the names foxtail and swan's neck come from. Its soft leaves also lack the usual teeth and spines.

Q135235.funFact: The rosette stays compact, around half a metre across, yet its spike of cream flowers can shoot up to 4 m. It comes from the Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico and rarely makes offsets, so most plants are raised from seed.

Q11684614.careNotes: One of the few aroids that grows well in medium light, away from the window.
Q11684614.funFact: Its genus, Aglaonema, has been grown in Asia as a bringer of good luck for centuries. The plants first reached the West in 1885, when they arrived at Kew Gardens in London.

Q4056964.careNotes: One of the few aroids that grows well in medium light, away from the window.
Q4056964.funFact: One of its old names is green-for-ten-thousand-years. In the wild it grows in tropical swamps and rainforests from Bangladesh and Thailand to Vietnam and southern China.

Q15313751.careNotes: One of the few aroids that grows well in medium light, away from the window.
Q15313751.funFact: Its genus has been kept in Asia as a bringer of good luck for centuries, yet it only reached the West in 1885, when the first plants arrived at Kew.

Q15313823.funFact: It grows wild on Nias and Sumatra. Its genus, Aglaonema, has been kept in Asia as a bringer of good luck for centuries, and first reached the West in 1885, when plants arrived at Kew.

Q11679534.careNotes: It grows in winter and rests in summer, when the leaves die back: keep it dry then.
Q11679534.funFact: Its narrow leaves curl into tight spirals like little springs, and its nodding green and yellow flowers give off a sweet scent reminiscent of vanilla. It grows wild in the Western and Northern Cape of South Africa.

Q51148.careNotes: Hardy: it dies back in winter and returns in spring. Cut the leaves at the base.
Q51148.funFact: Of all the alliums, it alone grows wild in both the Old World and the New. The Latin name blends Greek words for rush and leek, and in the Middle Ages it went by the name rush leek.

Q51077575.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q51077575.funFact: Wild only in Kalimantan, the Indonesian part of Borneo, it is rare in the shops, where it turns up either as the plain species or as the cultivars 'Dragonscale', 'Green Dragon' and 'Silver Dragon'.

Q4062814.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q4062814.funFact: Nobody knows where it grows truly wild, as it is only found in gardens and near human settlements. In Laos and Thailand it is kept at Buddhist temples because it is thought to bring good luck.

Q15314291.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q15314291.funFact: Cuprea refers to the copper sheen of its leaves, strongest on young ones, whose undersides are deep purple. The plant hunter Thomas Lobb brought it from Borneo to Europe in the 1850s for the Veitch nurseries.

Q15314264.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q15314264.funFact: Sold as purple sword, silver sword or baroque sword, it holds its leaves pointing upwards, up to about 1.5 metres. Wild plants come from northern New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago.

Q1484310.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q1484310.funFact: Its name has travelled with Austronesian languages across the Pacific: biga in the Philippines, via in Fiji and Madagascar, pia in Hawaii. The huge heart-shaped leaves also make handy umbrellas in a tropical downpour.

Q1320008.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q1320008.funFact: The species name odora refers to the flowers' sweet fragrance, which is strongest after dark and explains the common name night-scented lily. It grows wild across East and Southeast Asia, from Japan to Borneo.

Q15314453.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q15314453.funFact: Long sold as 'Black Velvet' and assumed to be a nursery hybrid, it is in fact a wild species, known only from dry, deeply shaded limestone cliffs in one wildlife reserve in Sabah, Malaysia.

Q2839184.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q2839184.funFact: Its wavy leaf edges reminded people of the rippling blade of the kris, a traditional sword, hence the name kris plant. In the wild it grows only in northern Mindanao in the Philippines.

Q2125255.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q2125255.funFact: Plants sold under this name seem not to be the true New Guinea species, a small green-leaved plant, but a sterile hybrid bred in France before 1897. Its name, 'Uhinki', was misspelled 'whinkii' in catalogues, which may be how the mix-up began.

Q15314868.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q15314868.funFact: The zebra in its name refers to the striped leaf stalks, not the leaves. In Tagalog it is called gabing tigre, or tiger taro, and it grows wild only on a handful of islands in the Philippines.

Q9148985.careNotes: It often drops its leaves and rests in winter, going back to its corm. Keep it barely moist and warm, and it regrows in the Growing season.
Q9148985.funFact: Despite its old name, amazonica, it is an artificial hybrid bred from two Asian species: Alocasia longiloba from Southeast Asia and the kris plant from the Philippines.

Q162137.funFact: Its other name, krantz aloe, comes from the Afrikaans word for a rocky cliff. In southern Africa it was planted round livestock pens as a living fence, and the aloes often outlast the pens, marking where old kraals once stood.

Q291572.funFact: Its name means 'juvenile', because early growers took the small plant for a young aloe. Nobody knew where it came from until 1982, when a few wild plants turned up on a tiny rocky ridge in south-west Kenya.

Q140021.funFact: Found wild only in the high Drakensberg of Lesotho, where snow often buries it in winter, it arranges its leaves in five neat spiral rows, with about 21 leaves to each full turn.

Q80079.careNotes: Pups grow around the base: cut them off with a few roots once they have four or five leaves, and pot them on their own.
Q80079.funFact: It comes from the Hajar Mountains of Oman and the UAE, but it has been grown around the world for so long, and wild plants are so hard to find, that some botanists think it began as a garden hybrid.

Q206532.careNotes: Deciduous and only a little hardy: it looks dead in winter, then resprouts late in spring. Keep it frost-free and nearly dry.
Q206532.funFact: Both its Latin name, Aloysia, and its old Spanish name, Hierba de la Princesa, were chosen to flatter Maria Luisa of Parma, Princess of Asturias. By 1797 this South American shrub had become a common sight in London greenhouses.

Q1493.careNotes: A bromeliad grown like a succulent: full sun and soil that dries between waterings. Keep a little water in its central cup while it's growing, and grow new plants from the leafy top of a shop-bought pineapple.
Q1493.funFact: In 18th-century Europe a pineapple was such a costly status symbol that hosts showed off the same fruit at dinner after dinner until it rotted. In the wild, hummingbirds do most of the pollinating.

Q26686.careNotes: It runs to seed quickly in heat and dry soil: keep it moist, and sow again for a fresh supply.
Q26686.funFact: Serbians say someone is "dill in every soup" where English speakers would say they have a finger in every pie. The Latin genus name, Anethum, comes from a Greek word once used for both dill and anise.

Q2452846.funFact: Anthurium joins the Greek words for flower and tail, after the spadix that sticks out from the middle. The glossy red or pink part that looks like a petal is really the spathe, a modified leaf.

Q15318639.careNotes: Its velvet leaves need high humidity to open without tearing: a humidifier or a glass cabinet helps.
Q15318639.funFact: Its pale veins look like a ribcage, so growers informally group it with the esqueleto anthuriums, from the Spanish for skeleton. In the wild it grows on shady limestone ledges in the rainforests of Chiapas, Mexico.

Q4067647.careNotes: Its velvet leaves need high humidity to open without tearing: a humidifier or a glass cabinet helps.
Q4067647.funFact: Wild plants grow on the edges of rainforests in Colombia and Panama, sometimes perched on trees as epiphytes. Its velvety leaves are traced with white veins, and after pollination the pale green spadix ripens into red berries.

Q4116566.funFact: The bird's nest name comes from its upright crown of leaves, which looks rather like a nest. Most plants sold under this name are actually hybrids rather than the true species.

Q1746442.funFact: Along with Anthurium andraeanum, it is the only anthurium with naturally bright red spathes, which is why so many colourful hybrids descend from these two.

Q12835882.careNotes: Its long, ribbed leaves need high humidity to open without tearing: a humidifier or a glass cabinet helps.
Q12835882.funFact: Its hanging leaves can reach several feet long, and its name honours Veitch, a long-running family of plant nurseries in Exeter founded by John Veitch. In the wild it is found only in Colombia, growing on other plants.

Q15321489.funFact: In the Amazon it grows perched on trees rather than in soil, letting its narrow strap leaves hang down as far as 2.4 m.

Q4067642.careNotes: Its velvet leaves need high humidity to open without tearing: a humidifier or a glass cabinet helps.
Q4067642.funFact: In Colombian rainforest it creeps up trees as an epiphyte, and its velvety leaves can reach about 1.2 m long. It honours Arthur Warocqué, a Belgian industrialist and horticulturalist, and was first collected in 1874 by Gustav Wallis.

Q156843.funFact: Squeeze the sides of a flower and its 'mouth' snaps open like a dragon's, which is how it got its name. Bumblebees are strong enough to prise the lips apart and climb in for pollen, and the seed pod that follows is shaped like a tiny skull.

Q3231986.funFact: The bright yellow part is mostly bracts, which hang on long after the short-lived true flowers have faded. It comes from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, and strong light, not day length, is what sets it blooming.

Q41793383.careNotes: Its stems trail: grow it in a hanging pot.
Q41793383.funFact: Flagelliformis means whip-shaped, after the long trailing stems that also earn it the name rattail. It was among the first cacti brought into European gardens, by 1690 or earlier, yet almost nothing is known about how it lives in the wild.

Q161070.careNotes: It likes a cool, bright room in winter (10 to 15 °C) and humid air; the lower branches drop in warm, dry air.
Q161070.funFact: Not a true pine at all, it is a cousin of the monkey-puzzle tree. Captain Cook hoped its tall, straight trunks would make masts for ships, but the timber proved not strong enough.

Q163675.funFact: Called Manryō in Japan, it is a traditional New Year decoration there, thanks to its red berries and a play on its name, and is often arranged alongside winter jasmine.

Q2062517.funFact: A wild shrub of the Canary Islands, it is the commonest member of its genus there, growing in sunny coastal scrub. Its fragrant white daisies open in the morning and close again at night.

Q39719918.funFact: DNA studies showed it is not a true aloe but closer to Haworthia and Astroloba, so it now sits alone in its own genus. In Sesotho it is called serelei, the slippery one.

Q1816048.careNotes: Its tuberous roots store water, so it copes with a dry spell, and it takes some sun.
Q1816048.funFact: The name foxtail fern is misleading: it is no fern at all, but a close relative of the asparagus we eat, native to southern Africa from Mozambique to South Africa.

Q1399941.careNotes: Its tuberous roots store water, so it copes with a dry spell. It sheds needles in dry air.
Q1399941.funFact: Despite the name, it is not a fern at all but a member of the asparagus family. Its feathery foliage is made of leaf-like cladodes, each barely a tenth of a millimetre thick, growing in clusters along barbed stems.

Q3239567.careNotes: It tolerates deep shade, cold rooms and neglect, but not wet feet.
Q3239567.funFact: Also called the bar-room plant, it is used in Japan to teach the seika style of ikebana. Its fleshy cream and maroon flowers seem to be pollinated mostly by fungus gnats.

Q1736890.careNotes: Water the soil, not the central rosette, where standing water rots the new fronds.
Q1736890.funFact: In Taiwan its young shoots, called shansu, are a traditional aboriginal vegetable, stir-fried or boiled, and popular enough now to turn up on chain restaurant menus. In Polynesia the fronds are cooked with coconut cream.

Q132514.funFact: Nicknamed sand dollar and sea urchin cactus, it is a squat, spineless disc only a few centimetres high. Bees pollinate it, and one species, Diadasia rinconis, does the job best.

Q637364.funFact: Instead of spines, its stem wears a dusting of tiny white hairs. The usually five ribs give young plants the star shape behind the genus name, Astrophytum, which means star plant.

Q133127.funFact: The largest and tallest of its genus, it can reach 2 metres high on Mexico's Central Plateau. The white woolly flecks it grows over its skin help protect it from the sun.

Q783868.careNotes: Glochids, its tiny hooked bristles, lodge in the skin: handle it with thick gloves or tongs.
Q783868.funFact: Subulata means awl-like, after the slender pointed leaves, up to 12 cm long, that it keeps on its stems. At home it grows high in the Peruvian Andes, above 3,000 m.

Q510340.careNotes: Its swollen base stores water, so it copes with long dry spells. It takes less direct sun than most succulents.
Q510340.funFact: Its swollen base is a water tank that can grow to 14 m around in the wild, earning it the name elephant's foot. Though sold as a ponytail palm, it is not a true palm, and plants 350 years old have been recorded in Mexico.

Q6395156.careNotes: It flowers in sun or part shade. Water the soil, not the leaves.
Q6395156.funFact: Cucullata means 'hooded'. This South American species is one of at least five parents of the familiar bedding wax begonia, a hybrid named for its thick, waxy leaves.

Q4880553.funFact: Like all begonias, it carries the name of Michel Bégon, a governor of the French colony that is now Haiti, chosen by the monk and botanist Charles Plumier. One relative, Begonia darthvaderiana, is named after the Star Wars villain.

Q2893846.funFact: Its silver spots are pockets of air trapped just under the leaf surface. One theory says they imitate butterfly eggs, putting butterflies off laying their own on a leaf that already looks taken.

Q2893849.funFact: It was first named from greenhouse plants of unknown origin, and only much later found growing wild in southern China and northern Vietnam. The dark cross-shaped mark on each leaf gives it its common name.

Q2893850.funFact: Rex begonias cross so freely that this one species sits in the family tree of more than 500 cultivars. It first reached England from Assam and was documented in 1857.

Q1021163.funFact: Like other billbergias, it holds rainwater in its leaf funnels, and these little pools can host tiny communities of animals, algae and water plants. The genus is named after the Swedish naturalist Gustaf Johan Billberg.

Q4925794.funFact: What looks like a little trunk is really an upright rhizome. It comes from New Caledonia and is now placed in the genus Oceaniopteris, with Blechnum gibbum as its older name.

Q159984.careNotes: It flowers best a little pot-bound and on the dry side. Bring it into a bright, cool room before frost.
Q159984.funFact: The bright purple 'petals' are really papery bracts wrapped around tiny white flowers, which is why it is called paperflower. Its species name, glabra, is Latin for bald.

Q2921547.careNotes: It flowers best a little pot-bound and on the dry side. Bring it into a bright, cool room before frost.
Q2921547.funFact: The bright colour is not petals at all. The true flowers are small, white and easy to miss, and each cluster is framed by showy modified leaves called bracts in white, red, mauve, purple or orange.

Q140288.careNotes: Its bulb sits half above the soil. Water only while its climbing stem is green, and keep it dry once the stem dies back.
Q140288.funFact: Its genus honours James Bowie, a 19th-century plant collector for Kew, and volubilis is Latin for twining. From a pale bulb perched on top of the soil it sends up a branching climbing stem that looks like green spaghetti.

Q134360.careNotes: Very thirsty and hungry in summer: water and feed it generously. Overwinter it cool and frost-free.
Q134360.funFact: The hardiest angel's trumpet against cold and drought, it grows in dry Andean valleys high enough to get light frosts. Moths pollinate it, drawn by the white flowers and a scent that strengthens towards evening.

Q27344.careNotes: It copes with part shade. Clip it in late spring and again in late summer.
Q27344.funFact: Box grows so slowly that its wood is extremely hard and has no visible grain, ideal for flutes, oboes and engraving blocks. Neanderthals in Italy carved digging sticks from it over 170,000 years ago.

Q10296092.careNotes: A tuber grown for its leaves: keep it warm (above 18 °C), humid and out of direct sun. The leaves die back in autumn; store the tuber dry and warm until spring, then pot it up again.
Q10296092.funFact: More than a thousand named cultivars descend from this one South American species. The genus name comes from keladi, a Malay word used for several plants in the arum family.

Q145930.funFact: Both marigold and Mary's gold were names given in honour of the Virgin Mary. The edible petals are still scattered over salads for colour or used in place of saffron, and were once a dye for cloth, food and cosmetics.

Q1693148.funFact: Every node that touches the ground can put down roots, which is how it spreads into dense mats. In Hong Kong it has gone wild on rooftops.

Q160121.careNotes: Keep the root ball moist while flower buds form in late summer, or they drop before opening.
Q160121.funFact: In the snowy mountains of northern Honshu, one variety spends winter buried under drifts up to 2.4 m deep and starts flowering as soon as the snow melts, earning it the Japanese name yuki-tsubaki, snow camellia.

Q2590046.careNotes: Keep the root ball moist while flower buds form in late summer, or they drop before opening.
Q2590046.funFact: Its seed oil is so close to olive oil in make-up that it is nicknamed 'Oriental olive oil'. In Japan it was first grown for that oil and only became a garden flower in the early 1600s.

Q163559.careNotes: Thirsty and hungry in summer: keep it moist and feed it well in full sun. Lift the rhizome, or protect it, before frost.
Q163559.funFact: Its hard, round black seeds look like shotgun pellets, hence the name Indian shot. They are dense enough to sink in water and tough enough to be fired through wood and still sprout.

Q1380.careNotes: It needs more warmth than tomatoes, and flowers best in the hottest spot you have.
Q1380.funFact: Birds are not bothered by capsaicin, the compound that makes chillies hot, so they eat the fruit and carry the seeds far and wide. The name pepper is a mistake: Europeans took the fiery fruit for a kind of black pepper.

Q15249818.careNotes: Usually sold as a bonsai: keep it bright, with some sun, and never let its shallow pot dry out. It likes humid air.
Q15249818.funFact: Also called the Philippine tea tree, it grows wild from India and Japan all the way to Cape York in Australia. In China it is a favourite plant for penjing.

Q221543.funFact: Each leaf is made of many pairs of leaflets shaped like a fish's tail fin, hence the name, and the pith of its trunk can be turned into a flour much like sago.

Q161093.careNotes: It loves heat and dislikes wet soil: let the top dry between waterings.
Q161093.funFact: Botanists once filed it under Vinca, and in the US it is still often sold by that old name. At home on the dry southern coasts of Madagascar it behaves like a weed, seeding itself freely along roadsides and in fallow fields.

Q133733.funFact: The genus honours William Cattley, a horticulturist who coaxed a plant collected in Brazil into bloom. John Lindley described the first species from that very plant in 1824.

Q312190.funFact: The shaggy white 'hair' that gives it its name is made of modified spines that shield the cactus from sun and frost. Hidden underneath are sharp yellow spines, so it is far less cuddly than it looks.

Q6653247.funFact: Its white flowers, up to 30 cm long, open at night and close again in the morning. In the wild it sometimes grows perched on trees and shrubs, and birds often choose it as a place to build their nests.

Q310887.funFact: Its big cream flowers open at night, for one night only, and matter greatly to the bats that pollinate them. The Wayuu people of La Guajira even use the cane-like wood inside its stems in wattle and daub building.

Q148960.funFact: John Medley Wood of the Durban Botanic Gardens found it in 1881 hanging from rocks on a South African mountain, and later sent a living plant to Kew. The little tubers that form along its stems probably explain the name rosary vine.

Q5069352.funFact: Also known as the cataract palm, it grows by rivers without a trunk, and its thin, bendy leaflets give floodwater little to push against. Its creeping stem anchors it even more firmly in place.

Q660200.careNotes: It copes with lower light than most palms, even a north window.
Q660200.funFact: It became a Victorian favourite because it could survive the dark, often unheated British homes of the day. Unusually for a palm, it can flower when barely 30 cm tall.

Q2948042.funFact: Its genus name, Chamaedorea, joins Greek words for 'on the ground' and 'gift', a nod to how low these palms grow and how easily their fruit can be reached. Each plant carries only male or only female flowers.

Q15248029.funFact: Long before it was a houseplant, the Maya grew it around their villages and temples, possibly for religious use. The specimen it was first described from was collected near Chichén Itzá.

Q161747.careNotes: A palm hardy to about −10 °C, so it can stay out on the balcony through most European winters.
Q161747.funFact: One of only two palms native to mainland Europe, it relies on a single known insect pollinator, a weevil. To lure it, the plant releases scent from its leaves rather than its flowers.

Q1164349.careNotes: It copes with a dry spell and lower light well. Brown tips often come from fluoride in tap water.
Q1164349.funFact: The baby plants hang from the same long stems that carry its flowers, putting down roots wherever they touch the soil. Before it settled in Chlorophytum in 1862, botanists had moved it through several genera, including Phalangium and Hollia.

Q15530181.funFact: Chinese writers were describing chrysanthemums around 500 BCE, and the first book devoted to them appeared in 1104. Today there are thought to be somewhere between 20,000 and 30,000 cultivars.

Q3500365.funFact: Alata means winged, a nod to its angled young stems, which are occasionally winged. Indoors it seldom flowers, but in its tropical American home it bears small purplish to black fruits.

Q2697953.funFact: Its old genus name, Cissus, comes from the Greek for ivy, and 'antarctica' simply points to its southern home. Aboriginal Australians ate its berries and drew drinking water from the young stems.

Q20686225.funFact: This Mediterranean mandarin first turned up in Italy in the early 1800s and is a parent of the clementine. Its pruned leaves are distilled for petitgrain oil.

Q465934.funFact: Its leaves look like two joined end to end, because the stalk is flattened into a second leaf-like wing. In old Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, workers rubbed the juice on their legs to keep off land leeches, so it was also called leech lime.

Q124344319.funFact: Its genus, Citrus, probably first evolved in the foothills of the Himalayas. Almost all everyday citrus fruits, from lemons to grapefruit, are hybrids descended from three wild species: mandarin, pomelo and citron.

Q500.funFact: A lemon is a hybrid of citron and bitter orange. It reached the Americas in 1493, when Christopher Columbus carried lemon seeds to Hispaniola on his voyages.

Q3748857.funFact: It is a cross between a kumquat and, most likely, a mandarin orange. The skin is so thin that growers in Florida snip each fruit from the tree by hand to keep it from tearing.

Q144921.funFact: As in other Cleistocactus species, its red tubular flowers barely open, with only the style and stamens poking out, and they stick out sideways from the woolly white column. It grows wild on steep, dry cliffs in the mountains of Tarija, Bolivia.

Q149094.careNotes: Not a true bulb: it's evergreen. A cool, drier rest (about 10 °C) in winter makes it flower; water again once the flower stalk is a hand high.
Q149094.funFact: The genus honours Lady Charlotte Clive, Duchess of Northumberland, who first grew it in England and supplied the flowers used to describe it. Miniata refers to cinnabar, the red of red lead, after the flower colour.

Q1345646.careNotes: It needs more light than most to keep its colours, including a few hours of direct sun, and drops leaves in draughts or when moved.
Q1345646.funFact: Its leaves vary so wildly in shape and colour that botanists kept naming it afresh, and one variety alone has about 250 synonyms. Growers have added more than 300 cultivars on top.

Q47685.careNotes: Keep its soil evenly moist and the air humid. Once mature, it can flower and set red berries.
Q47685.funFact: Arabica is itself a natural cross between two other coffee species, thought to have happened more than half a million years ago in East Africa, which left it with four sets of chromosomes.

Q39087854.careNotes: Tender and succulent: bring it into a bright room before frost, and let it dry between waterings.
Q39087854.funFact: The leaves smell like a blend of oregano, thyme and turpentine. Though native to Africa, Arabia and India, it reached the Americas from Spain, which is why one of its many names is Spanish thyme.

Q10881792.funFact: Linnaeus first put it in the basil genus. Its reds and purples come from anthocyanins, and the more light it gets, the more of these pigments it makes, at the expense of green chlorophyll.

Q227997.careNotes: A bog plant: keep the soil constantly moist, and it can stand in a shallow saucer of water while it's growing. Outdoors it dies back in the cold; store the tuber dry and frost-free.
Q227997.funFact: This is taro, one of the oldest crops people grow; esculenta is Latin for edible. The English word taro was borrowed from Māori after Captain Cook saw taro plantations in New Zealand in 1769.

Q15492457.funFact: Its genus was named by Linnaeus after Fabio Colonna, a 16th-century Italian botanist. Columneas grow on trees in the wild, and their bright tubular flowers can look like little fish, which is where the goldfish plant name comes from.

Q2717614.careNotes: It likes more warmth and humidity than most indoor trees.
Q2717614.funFact: Austronesian voyagers carried it across the Pacific as far as Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island. In Hawaii its fermented roots are distilled into a spirit called okolehao, and in many island rituals red and green leaves carry different meanings.

Q41611.careNotes: It runs to seed quickly in heat and dry soil: keep it moist, in part shade in summer, and sow again for a fresh supply.
Q41611.funFact: Its name may go back to the ancient Greek word for a bed bug, after its smell. About half a litre of its seeds was found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and since it does not grow wild in Egypt, that hints the Egyptians farmed it.

Q2716378.funFact: The white powder on its leaves, called farina, reflects sunlight and helps the plant save water. Oddly, rain and dew do not wash it off, yet a brush of the hand smudges it for good.

Q3448252.funFact: Wild plants grow among rocky quartz fields in the Little Karoo of South Africa. The name bear's paw comes from the small reddish teeth at the tip of each fuzzy leaf.

Q2705184.funFact: Round, grey, red-rimmed leaves shaped like coins or biscuits give it nicknames such as silver dollar plant and cookie plant. Wild plants grow on dry, rocky ground in South Africa's Succulent Karoo.

Q5182516.funFact: Muscosa is Latin for mossy, and its old name lycopodioides compares it to clubmoss. The tiny leaves pack so tightly round the stems that the shoots look square.

Q157299.funFact: Crassula comes from the Latin for thick, after its fleshy stems, which turn brown and bark-like with age but never become true wood. In the wild it spreads mainly by dropping branches that take root.

Q15482979.funFact: Like almost all crassulas grown at home, it comes from South Africa. The genus name is from the Latin crassus, meaning thick, after the plump succulent leaves.

Q1404147.funFact: Known as buttons on a string, rosary vine and bead vine, it has pairs of fleshy, powdery leaves fused together at the base. In strong sun it takes on a reddish colour.

Q165077.careNotes: A spring bulb: pot it in autumn and keep it cold (below 10 °C) and lightly moist while the roots form, then bring it into the light when shoots appear.
Q165077.funFact: Wild in the Alps, the Pyrenees and the Balkans, it also turns up in British grassland, from churchyards to roadside verges. The name vernus points to spring, when it flowers.

Q3496448.funFact: The firecracker name comes from its seed pods, which burst open in humid or rainy weather and scatter the seeds. The flowers are often threaded into strands with white jasmine for temple garlands and hair decorations.

Q5190674.careNotes: It has no central cup: keep the soil lightly moist instead.
Q5190674.funFact: Like every Cryptanthus, it is found wild only in Brazil, and its genus name is Greek for hidden flower.

Q15326022.funFact: The species name honours the landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx, and the alternating stripes on its leaves earn it the fishbone nickname. Like its relatives, it folds its leaves up at night, as if in prayer.

Q15326722.funFact: Its genus, Ctenanthe, was named in 1884 and grows mainly in Brazil. This species can reach 2 m tall, with oval leaves up to 30 cm long, heavily striped and mottled with yellow.

Q5191611.funFact: Its cream-striped cultivar 'Tricolor' looks so like Stromanthe 'Triostar' that the two are often mixed up. The tell is in the leaves: this one has more regular bands and a rounder shape.

Q5194465.funFact: Hyssopifolia means 'hyssop-leaved', after its fine, narrow leaves. One of its nicknames is Hawaiian heather, yet it comes from Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras, and in Hawaii it has become a serious weed.

Q50840600.careNotes: Its leaves rot in wet soil: water it only once the soil is dry right through, and give it some direct sun.
Q50840600.funFact: Its small white flowers smell of cinnamon, and each curved, banana-shaped leaf has see-through lines along its sides. It is also sold under the name fishhook senecio.

Q56646846.careNotes: An upright succulent rather than a vine: give it full sun and let the soil dry right through.
Q56646846.funFact: In the wild it creeps through rocky crevices and over exposed ledges on dry sandstone slopes of South Africa's Cape. Linnaeus first described it in 1767, under the name Cacalia repens.

Q50840601.careNotes: Its pearls rot in wet soil: water it only once the soil is dry right through, and give it some direct sun.
Q50840601.funFact: Each pea-sized leaf has a thin see-through stripe, called a window, that lets light inside, so the round, water-saving shape can still photosynthesise. The small white flowers are said to smell of cinnamon.

Q161517.careNotes: A cycad, not a palm. It wants bright light with some sun, and grows its new leaves all at once: don't move it while they're soft.
Q161517.funFact: Despite the name sago palm, it is not a palm at all but a cycad, an unrelated seed plant. The largest one in cultivation, at the Ryugeji Temple in Shimizu, Japan, stands about 8 m tall.

Q150055.careNotes: It grows and flowers in the cool seasons and rests in summer: keep it cool (10 to 15 °C) and fed while it flowers, water from below, and let it dry off once the leaves yellow.
Q150055.funFact: Despite a name meaning 'from Persia', it grows wild from Turkey to the Levant, not in Persia. After flowering, its stems bend to press the seed pods into the soil, and the pods only split open once they are underground.

Q843914.careNotes: It needs a cool autumn (about 10 °C at night), ideally outdoors, to flower. It's thirstier than most orchids.
Q843914.funFact: Cymbidium means little boat, after the shape of the lip. These are among the oldest orchids in cultivation, mentioned by Confucius and in a Chinese manuscript from around the 200s CE.

Q33913.careNotes: Tender and thirsty: full sun and plenty of water in summer, and a warm, bright room in winter.
Q33913.funFact: Beekeepers sometimes put lemongrass oil in swarm traps, because the scent draws in swarms. The plant rarely flowers or sets seed, so it is mainly spread by splitting clumps.

Q132993.careNotes: A marsh plant: keep it wet, even standing in a saucer of water, unlike almost any other houseplant.
Q132993.funFact: A new plant can be started by cutting off one of its leafy tops and standing it upside down in a glass of water. True to its sedge family roots, it is happy growing with its feet in shallow water.

Q2415732.careNotes: Hardy and tolerant: it copes with drier air, cool rooms and a shady balcony.
Q2415732.funFact: In eastern Asia it grows from cracks in seaside cliffs and rocky slopes. It has escaped from gardens so widely that it now grows wild in Mediterranean Europe, the Americas and Australia, where it is classed as a weed.

Q1549236.careNotes: It grows from a tuber: lift it after the first frost blackens the leaves, dry it, and store it frost-free in dry compost until spring.
Q1549236.funFact: The Aztecs grew it well before Europeans reached the Americas, and it arrived in Spain in 1798. Studies suggest the garden form is really a hybrid-like variant of another species, and the original wild plant is presumed extinct.

Q2789728.careNotes: Its furry rhizomes creep over the edge of the pot: keep them on the surface, never buried.
Q2789728.funFact: In the wild it clings to tree trunks, branches and mossy rocks in cool, damp places near the ocean, from Cape Verde and the Canaries to western Spain and Portugal. 'Canariensis' means from the Canary Islands.

Q5228130.careNotes: Its furry rhizomes creep over the edge of the pot: keep them on the surface, never buried.
Q5228130.funFact: The furry brown and yellow rhizomes that give it its name look just like rabbits' feet. In its native Fiji it grows perched on other plants rather than in soil.

Q2714635.careNotes: A hardy ground cover for a sunny balcony: it survives frost if its soil stays dry in winter.
Q2714635.funFact: Unlike many ice plants from South Africa, it can survive winters as cold as -29 °C, living outdoors in cities such as Denver and Chicago. When the weather turns cold, its leaves blush red.

Q133778.funFact: The name joins the Greek words for tree and life, since most of them grow perched on trees. Several appeared on Singapore's orchid banknotes of the late 1960s and 1970s.

Q636713.careNotes: It needs a cool, dry rest in winter to flower: stop watering once growth ends, until flower buds show.
Q636713.funFact: It is the state flower of Sikkim in India. In the wild it perches on trees or mossy limestone rocks in forests from the Himalayas and southern China to Indochina.

Q158984.funFact: At the University of Oxford, students wear carnations to their exams: white for the first, pink for those in between and red for the last. The genus name, coined by the Greek botanist Theophrastus, means 'divine flower'.

Q5274269.funFact: Its genus, Didymochlaena, is so distinct that botanists give it a fern family all of its own, Didymochlaenaceae. Its members grow from upright, scaly rhizomes and can reach 3 metres tall.

Q141806.funFact: Unlike many of its aroid relatives, such as monstera and philodendron, it neither climbs as a vine nor grows from a tuber. It shoots straight up in cane-like stems, which is where the name dumbcane comes from.

Q15629400.careNotes: It copes with dry spells better than most, and its flowers close in shade and dull weather.
Q15629400.funFact: It is named after Christian Friedrich Ecklon, a Danish collector who explored the plants of the Cape in the early 1800s. Because it grows fast all year and reacts to radiation, scientists use it in experiments and even as a UV indicator.

Q155825.careNotes: Don't set off the traps for fun: each one closes only a few times before it dies.
Q155825.funFact: In the wild it lives only in coastal bogs within about 100 km of Wilmington, North Carolina. A trap shuts only when two trigger hairs are touched in quick succession, so a falling raindrop will not set it off.

Q15397553.funFact: Its genus, Dischidia, is a close cousin of Hoya, and many of its members grow in ants' nests up in the trees. Some have even evolved hollow leaves, or leaves pressed flat with a space beneath, where the ants can live.

Q91265856.funFact: It climbs on trees in Mexican forests rather than living in desert, and its big pale flowers open at night with a strong sweet scent. Inside, the tasty fruit looks like kiwi, green with small black seeds.

Q80686286.funFact: Its leaves grow as round spears rather than flat straps, because the genes that would normally give a leaf a distinct top and underside are never switched on. In Brazil it is called St George's spear.

Q157952.careNotes: It grows slowly, and likes more sun and drier soil than other dracaenas.
Q157952.funFact: Cut its bark and it oozes a red resin, one of the substances known as dragon's blood. On Tenerife the Guanches worshipped one giant tree and hollowed its trunk into a small shrine; a storm brought it down in 1868.

Q133690.careNotes: Fluoride and salts in tap water brown its tips: use rain or filtered water.
Q133690.funFact: The English name comes from the stem's likeness to a maize stalk, while fragrans refers to its strongly scented flowers. In Tanzania the Chagga people call it masale and regard it as holy.

Q13539275.careNotes: Fluoride and salts in tap water brown its tips: use rain or filtered water.
Q13539275.funFact: Botanists now treat it as a variety of Dracaena reflexa, a tree from Madagascar and nearby islands whose fruit is an important food for the black-and-white ruffed lemur. Its many nicknames include Madagascar dragon tree.

Q85689460.funFact: Collected in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, it first did the rounds among growers as 'Mason Congo'. Potted plants are often a single big, stiff leaf, which explains the names whale fin and shark's fin.

Q135016.careNotes: Fluoride and salts in tap water brown its tips: use rain or filtered water.
Q135016.funFact: Back home in Madagascar, its fruit is an important food for the black-and-white ruffed lemur. The small white flowers open in midwinter and are strongly scented.

Q27686509.careNotes: Often grown in water: keep the roots covered, change the water whenever it looks cloudy, and use filtered or rain water.
Q27686509.funFact: Sold as lucky bamboo, it is not a bamboo at all but an African dracaena, and names hinting that it comes from China or Belgium are just as misleading. Its species name honours the German-English gardener Henry Frederick Conrad Sander.

Q5814069.careNotes: Fluoride and salts in tap water brown its tips: use rain or filtered water.
Q5814069.funFact: In the wild in West Africa it grows into a branching shrub, now and then 8 m tall, with glossy leaves freckled in cream or yellow and round berries that ripen orange to bright red.

Q65936984.funFact: It appears on the porch in Grant Wood's 1930 painting American Gothic. Another of its names, viper's bowstring hemp, recalls the tough leaf fibre that was once twisted into bowstrings.

Q1570130.careNotes: A sundew from the Cape: it needs no cold rest and keeps growing through winter on a sunny windowsill.
Q1570130.funFact: When an insect lands, the whole leaf slowly curls around it, bending through more than 180 degrees. The glue on its tentacles is so sticky that fresh strands can be drawn out to a metre long.

Q1535705.funFact: The name butterfly palm comes from its fronds, which arch up from many stems like wings. In Madagascar it was once a source of fibre for fishing nets, and one of its Malagasy names means fibre tree.

Q2413000.funFact: Agavoides means like an agave, after its thick, pointed, triangular leaves. The genus honours Atanasio Echeverría y Godoy, a botanical illustrator who worked on Flora Mexicana.

Q2783756.funFact: Its genus honours Atanasio Echeverría y Godoy, an illustrator who worked on Flora Mexicana, and 'elegans' means graceful. The rosettes stay only 5 to 10 cm high but can spread to half a metre across.

Q5332386.funFact: Lilacina means lilac-coloured, and its genus honours Atanasio Echeverría y Godoy, an 18th-century Mexican botanist famous for painting plants. It grows wild on high rocky ground in Nuevo León.

Q10269958.funFact: Its genus is named after Atanasio Echeverría y Godoy, an 18th-century Mexican artist who illustrated plants for the Flora Mexicana. Some echeverias are also the chosen egg-laying plants of particular butterflies.

Q5332391.funFact: Setosa means covered in stiff bristles, after the white hairs on its leaves. The genus is named for Atanasio Echeverría y Godoy, a botanical illustrator who worked on Flora Mexicana.

Q291973.funFact: Carlo Spegazzini collected it in the mountains of north-west Argentina in 1896, but later expeditions to the same area never found his plant again, and nobody knows whether that wild population survives.

Q142776.funFact: Its sweet-scented flowers, as long as 25 cm, sit at the end of long tubes, open at dusk and on hot days wilt by the following afternoon. In the 19th century it was crossed with other cacti to breed many big, colourful hybrids.

Q151275.funFact: Its white, funnel-shaped flowers open at night and are far longer than the little ball of a plant is tall, held out on a slender green tube. It is also known as the night-blooming hedgehog.

Q311230.funFact: Its huge scented flowers open at night and wilt before dawn. In Crazy Rich Asians, the characters throw parties just to watch one bloom, a plant known in Chinese as tan hua.

Q161809.careNotes: It tolerates lower light than most aroids, though its variegation fades there.
Q161809.funFact: It almost never flowers, wherever it grows, because a faulty gene stops it making the gibberellin hormones that trigger blooming. One of the last spontaneous flowerings in cultivation was reported in 1964.

Q549727.funFact: It starts life on the forest floor and climbs trees until it lives perched high up. Along the way its leaves change, so young leaves look quite unlike the mature ones on the same plant.

Q10923645.funFact: Its fuzzy leaves can be deep copper, reddish-green or plain green, and it spreads mostly by sending out runners rather than by seed. Kew was growing it from seed sent over from Colombia in 1845.

Q1368378.funFact: Its thick coat of woolly hairs suits life high on the Andean slopes, and in Peru the wool has been used to stuff pillows.

Q3272655.careNotes: Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you cut or repot it.
Q3272655.funFact: In the southern African savanna, birds eat its seeds and nest among its branches, and woodpeckers often move into the dead segments. Its light, solid wood has been used for doors, planks and boats.

Q5410474.careNotes: Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you cut or repot it.
Q5410474.funFact: Despite nicknames like candelabra cactus and false cactus, it is a spurge from South Asia, not a cactus. The crested cultivar 'Cristata' grows frilled, fan-like branches instead of upright ones.

Q148829.careNotes: Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you cut or repot it.
Q148829.funFact: The species name honours Baron Milius, a governor of Réunion who brought it to France in 1821. To the Bodo people of eastern India and Nepal, one of its varieties is the living form of their supreme god.

Q135673.careNotes: Keep it dry through the Dormant season. Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you repot it.
