Q135673.funFact: Shaped like a ribbed ball, it looks remarkably like Astrophytum asterias, an unrelated Mexican cactus: a case of convergent evolution in similar climates on two continents. Each plant carries only male or only female flowers.

Q208253.careNotes: Keep it above 15 °C and out of draughts, and let the top of the soil dry between waterings. Its red "petals" are leaves, which colour again only after long, fully dark nights from early autumn.
Q208253.funFact: The red 'petals' are really leaves called bracts, and they only colour up after long nights of darkness. The Aztecs called the plant cuetlaxōchitl and used it to make a red dye.

Q883685.careNotes: Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you cut or repot it.
Q883685.funFact: Its milky latex is rich in hydrocarbons, so the chemist Melvin Calvin proposed farming it for oil. Brazil's oil company Petrobras experimented with the idea in the 1980s, without much success.

Q3338078.careNotes: Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you cut or repot it.
Q3338078.funFact: Its red, slipper-shaped bracts explain names such as slipper flower and, in Mexico, zapatilla del diablo, the devil's slipper. It is tough enough that towns have planted it on landfills and toxic waste sites.

Q1257890.careNotes: Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves when you cut or repot it.
Q1257890.funFact: Nobody has ever seen it flower, it is known only from cultivation, and it may be a hybrid. In Gabon it is planted as a hedge and used as a ritual plant.

Q509542.careNotes: Hardy and happy cool: it suits an unheated room, a north window or a shady balcony.
Q509542.funFact: Bred at the Lizé Frères nursery in Nantes in 1912, it is a cross between Japanese fatsia and ivy, and its name simply glues the two parent genera together. It kept the ivy's five-lobed leaves but not its knack for climbing unaided.

Q203569.careNotes: Hardy and happy cool: it suits an unheated room, a north window or a shady balcony.
Q203569.funFact: The name fatsi is a rough version of the Japanese word for eight, after its lobed leaves. In Japan it is called yatsude, meaning eight fingers.

Q5856714.careNotes: It grows in late summer and autumn: water it then, and keep it almost dry in winter.
Q5856714.funFact: Its genus name comes from the Latin fauces, an animal's mouth, after the paired teeth along the leaf edges that make each pair of leaves look like open jaws. In strong sun the green leaves can turn purple.

Q147501.funFact: Latispinus is Latin for broad spine, after its flattened, often reddish spines. In the Mexican wild it usually grows in the shade of a nurse shrub or tree that shields it from the harsh sun.

Q4921039.funFact: A strangler fig, it often starts life perched on another tree and sends roots down to the ground until it can stand alone, by which time the host has been overwhelmed. In Florida it set no seed until foreign fig wasps arrived to pollinate it.

Q1405636.funFact: Its aerial roots drop to the ground and thicken into new trunks, so one tree can spread like a small forest. Nearchus, an admiral of Alexander the Great, described a banyan by the Narmada River said to shelter 7,000 men.

Q275160.funFact: It is the official tree of Bangkok. Its flowers can be pollinated only by one particular kind of wasp, which lives in partnership with the tree.

Q11888321.funFact: In the wet forests from southern Thailand to Borneo, the wild species is a strangler fig that can reach 30 metres tall. The compact 'Alii' sold as a houseplant is one of its cultivars.

Q36146.careNotes: Hardy and deciduous: it drops its leaves in winter and can stay outdoors in a sheltered spot. A snug pot helps it fruit.
Q36146.funFact: It may be the first plant people ever cultivated: sterile figs found in a Neolithic village near Jericho date to around 9400 BC, earlier than domesticated wheat and barley.

Q406938.funFact: You can tell male and female plants apart by their leaves: big and round on females, smaller and longer on males. Turn one over and the underside is golden yellow, speckled with black.

Q160576.funFact: In Meghalaya, India, people guide its aerial roots across ravines until they grow into living bridges. Before the Brazilian rubber tree took over in the late 1800s, it was the main tree tapped for rubber in Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula.

Q1498748.careNotes: Wipe the big leaves now and then so they catch more light, and turn the pot a quarter when you water so it grows straight.
Q1498748.funFact: Its leaves are wide at the tip and pinched in the middle, like a lyre or fiddle, which also gives it names such as banjo fig. Outdoors it can grow into a tree up to 12 metres tall.

Q714180.careNotes: Usually sold as a bonsai: its shallow pot dries out fast, so check it often and never let it dry right through.
Q714180.funFact: Its aerial roots drop from the branches and can thicken into extra trunks. Planted abroad it only sets seed once its own pollinating fig wasp arrives: in Rio de Janeiro's parks, where it had grown since the 19th century, seedlings first appeared in the 1970s.

Q2360517.careNotes: Never let it dry out: its thin leaves crisp quickly. It climbs walls with small aerial roots.
Q2360517.funFact: 'Pumila' means dwarf, after its tiny leaves. Its aerial roots ooze a clear latex that sets hard and glues the stems to walls, and in Taiwan the fruit of one variety is made into aiyu jelly.

Q3071706.funFact: A branch of the tree the Buddha is said to have sat under was planted at Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, in 288 BCE. It still grows there, the oldest living flowering plant known to have been planted by people.

Q50841020.funFact: Like every fig, it hides its tiny flowers inside the fig itself, where only minute wasps crawling in through a small opening at the tip can pollinate them. Each kind of fig depends on one or a few wasp species of its own.

Q11332399.funFact: Like every fig, its flowers are hidden inside the fruit and pollinated by tiny wasps that crawl in through a small opening. Each fig species depends on one or a few wasp species of its own.

Q144956.careNotes: It collapses dramatically when dry and recovers after a drink, but repeated wilting weakens it. It loves humid air: a terrarium suits it.
Q144956.funFact: It is called the nerve plant after the fine web of white or pink veins on its leaves. It is also known for dramatically 'fainting' when it runs dry, then perking up again after a drink.

Q13158.careNotes: It grows well in hanging baskets and window boxes, where the fruit stays clean. Pick the fruit as soon as it's red.
Q13158.funFact: Ananassa means pineapple, after the fruit's flavour. The garden strawberry is a cross between a Chilean and a North American species, first raised in Brittany in the 1750s, and each 'seed' on its skin is really a tiny fruit in its own right.

Q164101.careNotes: Unlike most of these, it prefers part shade and moist soil: an east-facing balcony suits it. It's one of the hardiest fuchsias.
Q164101.funFact: According to tradition, the English nurseryman James Lee spotted it on a sailor's windowsill, paid a small fortune for it and sold many plants raised from that one. It now runs wild in Irish hedgerows and is the emblem of West Cork.

Q1072101.careNotes: Fussy: it drops its buds if moved, left dry or kept below 16 °C. It wants warmth, humid air and lime-free water.
Q1072101.funFact: It reached England from the Cape in 1744, and nobody could propagate it until a Mile End gardener managed it in 1757, after which each plant fetched five guineas. The name cape jasmine comes from the old belief that it was South African.

Q16746629.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q16746629.funFact: It grows among pebbles on flat, stony ground by South Africa's Gamtoos River, where it is hard to spot. At the edges of its range it merges gradually into its much larger relative, Gasteria nitida.

Q1439759.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q1439759.funFact: Gasterias are named after their stomach-shaped flowers, gaster being Greek for stomach, while their thick tongue-shaped leaves explain names like ox tongue.

Q775301.careNotes: It copes with dry spells better than most, and its flowers close in shade and dull weather.
Q775301.funFact: The genus honours Theodore of Gaza, a 15th-century scholar who translated the plant writings of Theophrastus from Greek into Latin. Its flowers are sun-seekers, closing up in shade or when the sky clouds over.

Q746928.careNotes: Water at the edge of the pot, not into the crown, which rots.
Q746928.funFact: Cultivated gerberas all trace back to this South African daisy, crossed with another species in Cambridge around 1890. It features on the flag of Mpumalanga province.

Q50841675.funFact: It is grown for its fiery yellow-orange flower heads, held on straight stems just above the leaves, which give it the names eternal flame and saffron-coloured calathea. It comes from eastern Brazil.

Q90458733.funFact: In the Peruvian Amazon its leaves are used to wrap brown sugar. Like other prayer plants, it folds its leaves together at night and opens them out again in the morning.

Q50841683.funFact: Like other prayer plants, it lifts and folds its leaves at night and opens them again at dawn. New leaves come up rolled, showing their pinkish-red undersides, and it is also known as cathedral windows.

Q80714198.funFact: Its genus, Goeppertia, honours the German botanist and palaeontologist Heinrich Göppert. Many of its species were counted as calatheas until recently, but they can be told apart by their rosette-shaped flower clusters.

Q50841689.funFact: According to Marantaceae expert Helen Kennedy, most 'pinstripe calatheas' on sale are other species. The true one dropped out of cultivation before the mid-1990s, and the colour of its flowers is still unknown.

Q50841692.funFact: The dark reddish-purple undersides of its leaves are an adaptation to the dim light of the Amazon forest floor where it grows wild. It is still often sold under its old name, Calathea roseopicta.

Q50841693.funFact: Its species name means red beard, from the Latin rufus and barba, and it is unusual in its genus for the soft, fur-like texture under its leaves. It comes from Bahia in northeastern Brazil.

Q50841699.funFact: Plant hunter Richard Pearce found it near Cuenca, Ecuador, in 1862 and named it after his employers, the Veitch nursery. A Peruvian plant with the same leaf pattern was long mistaken for it.

Q80714465.funFact: Its flower bracts open white and slowly darken to deep purple, and the creamy flowers inside tend to stay shut until a pollinator pushes them open. The species name honours the plant collector Józef Warszewicz.

Q80714550.funFact: The species name means 'striped like a zebra', after the lime-green veins and edges etched onto its dark green leaves, which are dark red underneath.

Q39719922.funFact: The first written record of it is in the diary of Simon van der Stel, first Governor of the Cape, from a journey to Namaqualand in 1685. Sunbirds drinking its nectar are probably its main pollinators.

Q3574180.funFact: Also called mother-of-pearl plant, it owes the name ghost plant to the pale coating on its leaves, which break off so easily that it is nicknamed porcelain succulent. The plant is also eaten as a vegetable.

Q2710056.funFact: 'Lingulata' is Latin for tongue-shaped. In the wild it is an epiphyte, living perched on trees in rainforests from southern Mexico to central South America rather than rooted in soil.

Q144882.funFact: Its pale, curved spines are what earned it the name spider cactus. The species name honours J. Baldi, an acquaintance and supporter of the botanist Carlos Spegazzini, who first described it in 1905.

Q137994.careNotes: The coloured top has no chlorophyll: it lives only grafted onto the green cactus below. Give it bright light, but not harsh midday sun.
Q137994.funFact: The bright red, orange or yellow moon cactus is a mutant with no chlorophyll at all, so it cannot feed itself and must be grafted onto a green cactus that does the work. The wild species is a small grey-green cactus from Paraguay and Bolivia.

Q9268236.funFact: Soft purple hairs cover its leaves and stems, which is what gives it a velvety feel. The name aurantiaca means orange, after the usual colour of its flowers.

Q247743.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q247743.funFact: The tips of its leaves are see-through. In the harsh sun of South Africa's Eastern Cape it grows mostly buried in sand, with only those clear tips showing above the ground.

Q247484.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q247484.funFact: In the wild it grows mostly buried in sand, with only the translucent 'windows' at its leaf tips showing above the surface under the bright sun. Cymbiformis means 'boat-shaped', after its leaves.

Q64524505.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q64524505.funFact: Attenuata means tapering, after its narrow leaves banded with raised white bumps. It is often mistaken for the rarer Haworthiopsis fasciata, but that species only has bumps on the underside of its leaves.

Q39865423.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q39865423.funFact: Most plants sold under this name are really its lookalike, Haworthiopsis attenuata. The true species has smooth inner leaf faces, with white bands only on the outside, and grows in the acidic fynbos sands near Port Elizabeth.

Q39865426.careNotes: Unlike most succulents, it prefers bright light out of hot midday sun: an east or west window. Leaves turn red or brown in too much sun.
Q39865426.funFact: Its genus name, Haworthiopsis, means 'like Haworthia'. It was split off from Haworthia in 2013, once DNA studies showed the old group of plants did not hang together.

Q26354.careNotes: Hardy and happiest cool: a cool room, a north window or a shady balcony. In a warm, dry room it gets spider mites.
Q26354.funFact: The name means roughly the clinging plant that coils in spirals: hedera is the old Latin word for ivy, from a root meaning to seize, and helix is Greek for spiral.

Q106906298.funFact: Actinophyllum means 'with radiating leaves'. In Australian rainforests its red flower spikes, up to 2 metres long, feed nectar-eating birds, and its leaves are a favourite food of Bennett's tree-kangaroo.

Q65940871.funFact: In Chinese it is called goose-sole vine. In very humid conditions it sends down aerial roots that turn into ordinary roots once they reach the soil.

Q159534.careNotes: Tender: keep it above 10 °C. It needs more water than most, and drops its buds if it dries out.
Q159534.funFact: It has never been found in the wild: a 2024 study showed that Polynesians created it by crossing two island hibiscuses whose wild homes, Vanuatu and Tahiti, are more than 4,000 km apart.

Q757257.careNotes: Plant it with the top third of the bulb above the soil. After flowering, keep the leaves growing and fed; a cooler spell on the dry side brings it back into flower.
Q757257.funFact: Though sold as amaryllis, these bulbs belong to a separate American genus; true Amaryllis comes from South Africa. Hippeastrum means 'knight's star', and nobody knows for sure what its author had in mind.

Q11072005.funFact: Its genus, Homalomena, seems to take its name from a garbled translation of a Malay plant name, rendered in Greek as flat moon. Many of its relatives smell strongly of anise.

Q146290.careNotes: It tolerates shade and dry air better than most palms.
Q146290.funFact: Queen Victoria grew kentias in all her homes and asked for them to stand around her coffin as she lay in state. Potted kentias also decorated the palm court café aboard the Titanic.

Q311190.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q311190.funFact: 'Australis' is Latin for southern. Its sweet, nectar-rich flowers are pollinated by a small butterfly called the southern grass-dart, and its leaves feed the caterpillars of two crow butterflies.

Q134347.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q134347.funFact: The thick, star-shaped flowers look as if they were moulded from wax or porcelain, which gives the plant both its common names. They can make so much nectar that it drips.

Q1632094.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q1632094.funFact: Like all hoyas, it belongs to a genus named in 1810 after Thomas Hoy, gardener to the Duke of Northumberland. The thick, waxy flowers these plants produce give them their other common name, waxflowers.

Q292176.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q292176.funFact: Its thick heart-shaped leaves have earned it the name lucky-heart, and in Europe it is sold for Valentine's Day. The flowers give off their scent at night.

Q18073653.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q18073653.funFact: Its genus, Hoya, is named after Thomas Hoy, gardener to the Duke of Northumberland. Hoyas are mostly climbing vines that rarely root in the ground, and their stems twine to the left.

Q1632100.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q1632100.funFact: Its small flowers smell of cinnamon. In the wild, from Thailand to Borneo, Java, Sumatra and the Philippines, it is an epiphytic climber, clambering over other plants rather than rooting in the ground.

Q1632106.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q1632106.funFact: Its genus was named in 1810 by the botanist Robert Brown in honour of Thomas Hoy, gardener to the Duke of Northumberland. Hoyas are known as waxflowers for their fleshy, waxy blooms.

Q10648661.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q10648661.funFact: Its genus is named after Thomas Hoy, gardener to the Duke of Northumberland. Hoyas are known as waxflowers for their fleshy, waxy blooms, and most climb or scramble over trees and rocks, rarely rooting in the ground.

Q1632109.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q1632109.funFact: Like most hoyas, it lives perched on trees or rocks and rarely roots in the ground. The genus is named after Thomas Hoy, who was gardener to the Duke of Northumberland.

Q1632113.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q1632113.funFact: Native to the Philippines, where it climbs as a vine perched on trees, it has its flowers pictured on the Philippine five-centavo coin. It is sometimes confused with Hoya carnosa.

Q18074136.careNotes: Don't cut off the short spurs where flowers grew: it flowers again on the same ones.
Q18074136.funFact: Hoyas are climbing vines that seldom put roots into the ground, living instead on trees or rocks. Their stems twine to the left as they climb and carry a milky white latex.

Q1633949.careNotes: Keep it drier and cooler in winter. It scorches in hot midday sun more than most succulents.
Q1633949.funFact: Its genus honours Justus van Heurne, a Dutch missionary said to be the first European to collect Cape plants, though the collector misspelt his name. Huernia flowers lure flies with a smell of carrion.

Q157428.careNotes: A spring bulb: pot it in autumn and keep it cold (below 10 °C) and lightly moist while the roots form, then bring it into the light when shoots appear.
Q157428.funFact: Ants help plant its seeds. Each seed comes with a small white food parcel attached, and ants carry the seeds back to their nests to eat it, leaving the seed to sprout underground.

Q159219.careNotes: An outdoor shrub, and a thirsty one in summer. It wants part shade and shelter from hot afternoon sun; in acid soil, blue kinds stay blue.
Q159219.funFact: Blue, purple, pink and red flowers all come from one single pigment. In acid soil the plant takes up aluminium, which pulls the colour towards blue, while alkaline soil gives pink or even red.

Q5959593.funFact: The genus name combines the Greek for under and house, because the flowers hide beneath their bracts. The leaves look as if someone flicked paint across them, and the spots often run together into larger patches.

Q2391577.careNotes: It takes more sun than busy Lizzie but prefers morning sun and afternoon shade: an east-facing balcony. It wilts fast when dry.
Q2391577.funFact: First collected in Papua in 1884, it quickly became a greenhouse favourite. Botanists later found that fifteen other New Guinea impatiens gathered after it were all just forms of this one species.

Q654064.careNotes: Unlike most balcony flowers, it wants shade or morning sun only: a north- or east-facing balcony. It wilts fast when dry.
Q654064.funFact: Its name honours Horace Waller, a British missionary, and its ripe seed pods burst open to fling out seeds. Breeder Claude Hope in Costa Rica turned the wild East African plant into one of the world's favourite bedding plants.

Q13217438.careNotes: Grown for its silver leaves: it likes it dry and takes poor soil. Pinch out the flower buds to keep it compact.
Q13217438.funFact: Some wool carder bees collect the white felt that coats its leaves and stems to build their nests. In the wild it clings to cliffs and rocky shores around the Mediterranean.

Q515610.funFact: It has been grown for so long that its true homeland is uncertain, and it had naturalised so thoroughly in Europe that Linnaeus believed it was native to Switzerland. Its flowers release their scent at dusk, so they are picked at night for perfume.

Q282635.careNotes: It flowers in late winter and spring after a cool autumn outdoors; kept indoors all the time, it rarely sets buds.
Q282635.funFact: Polyanthum means many-flowered, and pink buds open into scented white stars. In the wild it climbs through valleys and forests in the mountains of southwest China and Myanmar.

Q1356614.careNotes: Tender: bring it into a bright room above 10 °C for winter.
Q1356614.funFact: Its flowers open in the evening and close again by morning. As sampaguita it is the national flower of the Philippines, where the blossoms are strung into garlands sold outside churches.

Q3303690.funFact: The 'shrimps' are overlapping bracts, not petals; the real flowers are the thin white tubes poking out of them. Hummingbirds are its usual pollinators, and the species name honours the American botanist Townshend Stith Brandegee.

Q146569.funFact: Its defences contain silica harder than mammal tooth enamel, and they make grazing animals take smaller bites. Even a cut leaf can sprout new plantlets straight from its surface.

Q132145.careNotes: Sold in flower, it sets buds again after a spell of long nights, as poinsettias do.
Q132145.funFact: A short-day plant, it only sets flowers once the nights grow long, which is why it blooms in winter and is sold as Christmas kalanchoe. The genus name was adapted from a Chinese name for one of its relatives.

Q311176.funFact: Rows of tiny plantlets form along its leaf edges and can grow roots while still attached, then drop off to start new plants. In the wild it comes from one river valley and a mountain range in south-west Madagascar.

Q137831.funFact: Tiny plantlets form along the tips of its leaves, each able to become a new plant, hence the name mother of millions. Far from Madagascar, hummingbirds in the American tropics sometimes pollinate it.

Q146646.funFact: The blue-green leaves, whose scalloped edges give it the name lavender scallops, have a microscopically waxy surface that makes water bead up and roll off, so they stay self-cleaning.

Q1625573.funFact: Laetivirens means lushly green: unlike its look-alike K. daigremontiana, its leaves have no spots or bands on the back. It was once thought to be a hybrid of that plant and K. laxiflora.

Q1598303.funFact: A member of its genus, Kalanchoe, was among the first plants sent into space, delivered to the Soviet Salyut 6 station in 1979. Kalanchoes open their flowers by growing new cells on the inner face of the petals.

Q138187.funFact: Most plants sold under this name are really a look-alike, Kalanchoe luciae, as the true species is rare in cultivation. It is one of the few succulents that flower only once and then die, and its round leaves stand upright on edge.

Q142606.funFact: Its Chinese name means moon rabbit ear, and the brown-tipped leaf edges earned it the name chocolate soldier. In Madagascar, a panda plant flowering for you is said to foretell wealth for your household.

Q42751825.funFact: Nicknamed mother-in-law's cushion, it is one of the most popular cacti in collections, yet it is endangered and perhaps gone from the wild in central Mexico, hit by poaching and by the building of a dam and reservoir.

Q332469.funFact: Its flowers change colour once pollinated, usually from yellow towards orange, pink or red, which is thought to tell insects which blooms still hold a reward. They smell of tutti frutti with a peppery edge.

Q26006.careNotes: It takes part shade and light frost. Clip it in summer to keep its shape.
Q26006.funFact: Rome's second emperor, Tiberius, wore a laurel wreath in stormy weather, because Romans believed the tree was immune to lightning, partly because laurel crackles so loudly when it burns.

Q42081.funFact: Despite the name English lavender, it is native to the Mediterranean, and angustifolia simply means narrow-leaved. The popular cultivar 'Munstead' is named after Munstead Wood in Surrey, the home of Gertrude Jekyll.

Q1450735.careNotes: Less hardy than English lavender: give it shelter or a frost-free spot in winter.
Q1450735.funFact: The Romans already knew this toothed-leaved lavender. The word lavender itself is thought to come from the Latin lavare, to wash, after blue infusions of the plant used for bathing.

Q1342976.careNotes: Less hardy than English lavender: give it shelter or a frost-free spot in winter.
Q1342976.funFact: Its species name goes back to the Greek botanist Dioscorides, who named it after the Stoechades Islands. The purple 'ears' on top of each flower head are sterile bracts with no flowers between them.

Q3497414.funFact: Its species name, socialis, means 'growing in colonies'. The genus honours Carl Friedrich von Ledebour, the botanist who published the first complete flora of Russia, although this bulb comes from South Africa's Eastern Cape.

Q133283.careNotes: Water only while it grows, from late summer into autumn, and lightly in spring. Never water while a new pair of leaves forms inside the old one: let the old pair shrivel away first.
Q133283.funFact: The name joins the Greek words for stone and face. The explorer William Burchell found the first one in 1811, when he bent down to pick up what he took for an oddly shaped pebble.

Q2632856.funFact: Its round, fan-shaped leaf is the unofficial national leaf of the Philippines, where the palm is called anahaw and its leaves are used to thatch roofs and wrap food. The tree only flowers once it is very old.

Q158858.funFact: In the wild, from Malawi and Zambia down to South Africa, its flowers are blue to violet. The white, pink, magenta and purple forms spilling from window boxes are the result of garden selection.

Q135499.careNotes: A jewel orchid, grown in soil rather than bark: a peat-free houseplant mix with bark, kept evenly moist, in shade. It's grown for its leaves more than its flowers.
Q135499.funFact: Until 2013 it was thought to be the only species in its genus, when a second was described from the Philippines. It is grown for its velvety maroon leaves with red veins, and roots on the forest floor rather than in trees.

Q42954007.funFact: Also known as Vriesea splendens, it reached Europe from Trinidad, Venezuela and the Guianas in 1840, and is named flaming sword for the flat, bright red flower spike rising from its banded rosette.

Q149788.funFact: It belongs to the nightshade family, alongside the potato and tomato, and was once classed in Solanum. The name honours Barthélémy Victor Rantonnet, a 19th-century French horticulturist.

Q143453.funFact: Its soft white 'powder puff' is made of hair-like spines that hide hooked central spines beneath. In the wild it grows on canyon walls and volcanic rock in north-central Mexico, often tucked under shrubs.

Q134530.funFact: In the wild in central Mexico it is one of the most common and most variable cacti in its genus. A crested form sold as 'Cristata' goes by the nickname brain cactus.

Q4043667.funFact: The species name, vetula, means little old one, and the stems look like tiny thimbles. Because it breaks into pieces that root at the slightest touch, one nurseryman reckons it is probably the most commonly grown mammillaria.

Q144980.funFact: The white down and fine white spines covering its round stems suit its name, old lady cactus. Its reddish purple flowers sometimes form a complete ring around the top of the plant.

Q283486.funFact: What look like white feathers are its spines, fringed with long hairs laid out like the barbs of a bird's feather. That fluffy coat shields the plant from the fierce desert sun of north-eastern Mexico.

Q290002.funFact: It was first described in 1838 by James Forbes, gardener to the Duke of Bedford, from cacti he had bought in Europe a few years before. In the wild it grows only in the Mexican states of Guerrero and Morelos.

Q3018376.careNotes: Tender: bring it into a bright room above 10 °C for winter.
Q3018376.funFact: Below ground it keeps fat tuberous roots stocked with water and starch, which help it ride out drought. Although called Brazilian jasmine, it is no relation of true jasmine, and it grows wild only in Rio de Janeiro state.

Q6754829.careNotes: Easier than calatheas: it copes better with ordinary household humidity.
Q6754829.funFact: Its leaves lie flat by day and fold upright at night, like hands in prayer. The small flowers have a trigger that deposits and collects pollen in one quick curl, and it fires only once.

Q10475339.careNotes: Keep it in one place once buds form: moving it drops them. It likes cool winters (about 13 °C) and more humidity than hoyas.
Q10475339.funFact: A favourite of bridal bouquets, hence the name Hawaiian wedding flower, it is not a jasmine at all but a climber from Madagascar. As its waxy flowers age they turn yellow and their rich scent goes sour.

Q148396.funFact: Bees love its flowers, hence Melissa, Greek for honey bee. The second name, officinalis, means 'of the shop', after the apothecaries who once sold it to their customers.

Q160114.careNotes: Vigorous and thirsty: give it a pot of its own and keep it moist. It takes part shade.
Q160114.funFact: It was an important cash crop in Connecticut during the American Revolution, when mint tea was popular because it escaped tax. The spear in its name refers to its pointed leaf tips.

Q17251563.funFact: What look like its pink petals are really sterile, modified stamens. The flowers open only in daytime sun and stay shut at night and on cloudy days, hence the British name heart-leaved midday flower.

Q17107423.funFact: Like most ferns, plants in its genus, Microsorum, grow from rhizomes rather than true roots. Some of its relatives live on rocks in fast-flowing streams.

Q2344941.careNotes: It likes it cool and humid, with the mix never fully dry.
Q2344941.funFact: Just five species make up this genus of pansy orchids, found wild from Costa Rica to Peru. Their flowers look much like those of Miltonia, but each pseudobulb carries only one leaf.

Q500991.careNotes: It climbs or trails: give it a moss pole for bigger leaves with more holes, or let it hang.
Q500991.funFact: The oval holes in its leaves give it the name Swiss cheese plant, and it also goes by five holes plant and monkey mask plant. In the wild this climbing vine is common along low-lying river valleys in Central and South America.

Q161077.careNotes: Give it a moss pole or stake: it's a climber, and leaves grow bigger and more split once its aerial roots have something to hold. Tuck the aerial roots into the pole or the soil rather than cutting them.
Q161077.funFact: "Deliciosa" means delicious, after its edible fruit, which tastes of pineapple and jackfruit and gives it the name fruit salad plant. Unripe, the fruit is full of needle-like oxalate crystals that irritate the mouth.

Q11785280.careNotes: A shingling climber: its young leaves lie flat against a plank or bark. Give it something to climb and it matures into split leaves.
Q11785280.funFact: Young plants press patterned leaves flat against a tree trunk like shingles, then switch to large split leaves as they climb. Dubia means doubtful: botanists first placed it, uncertainly, in another genus.

Q11785296.funFact: Its genus name, Monstera, comes from the Latin for monstrous or abnormal, after the natural holes in the leaves. Monsteras climb trees using hook-like aerial roots, and ones hanging to the ground have measured up to 30 m.

Q11785298.funFact: Its genus name comes from the Latin for 'monstrous' or 'abnormal', after the holes in the leaves of most species. Monsteras climb trees using hook-like aerial roots, and roots hanging to the ground have been measured at 30 m.

Q132970.careNotes: Thirsty and hungry: keep the soil moist while it's growing, and feed it at full strength. Its big leaves tear in draughts, which is harmless.
Q132970.funFact: It was one of the first plants people domesticated, possibly at first for its fibre or edible male bud rather than its fruit. Wild fruits are packed with hard seeds, which in the dessert bananas bred from it have shrunk to tiny black specks.

Q159562.careNotes: A spring bulb: pot it in autumn and keep it cold (below 10 °C) and lightly moist while the roots form, then bring it into the light when shoots appear.
Q159562.funFact: It is named after Armenia, part of its wild range in the woods and meadows from Greece and Turkey to the Caucasus. It first appeared in European gardens in 1871.

Q287064.funFact: Both its scientific and English names come from its edible dark purple berries, which look like bilberries and are sold as food in Mexico. Growers also value it as a fast-growing rootstock for grafting other cacti.

Q6122027.funFact: Its blue-black berries are steeped in alcohol to make mirto, a liqueur, and its small leaves carry a fragrant essential oil.

Q27498.careNotes: A spring bulb: pot it in autumn and keep it cold (below 10 °C) and lightly moist while the roots form, then bring it into the light when shoots appear.
Q27498.funFact: The Welsh call it Cennin Pedr, or Peter's leek, and it is the national flower of Wales. One of England's great wild stands grows along the River Dove in Farndale, in the North York Moors.

Q6965683.careNotes: Paperwhites need no cold spell: pot them up and they flower in a cool, bright room.
Q6965683.funFact: Its scent holds a compound shared with only a few plants, roses among them, that people can barely smell but honeybees detect easily. It is grown in southern France for its essential oil.

Q10646907.funFact: Its plump orange flowers look like little goldfish, or clogs, which gives it both common names. Some gardeners call it the garibaldi plant, after the California garibaldi, a sea fish it resembles.

Q3338220.funFact: Just before it flowers, the heart of the rosette flushes bright red, which is why it is called the blushing bromeliad. In the wild it grows only in Brazil.

Q217530.funFact: The name monkey cups seemed far-fetched to one National Geographic writer until, in Sarawak, a freed pet orangutan took a pitcher he offered and neatly drank it down. Some of the largest species occasionally trap frogs or small mammals.

Q161139.funFact: About two-thirds of cats react to it, thanks to nepetalactone, a compound that also repels insects. The name cataria simply means of cats, from the medieval Latin herba cattaria.

Q1040814.funFact: Its underground rhizome forms a string of small tubers, hence names like tuber ladder fern. It is not fussy about a home, turning up on tree bark, rock faces, ditches and even abandoned ruins.

Q136883.funFact: The Boston fern is a mutation: according to one account, its arching fronds were spotted in 1894 in a shipment of ordinary upright sword ferns sent from Philadelphia to Boston.

Q16986427.funFact: Its genus, Nephrolepis, also includes the Boston fern, and one species from Borneo grows long, narrow fronds that can reach nine metres.

Q155833.funFact: The genus name comes from the Greek for water, as it grows wild along rivers and streams. After Galveston, Texas, planted it widely following the 1900 hurricane, the island became known as the Oleander City.

Q38859.careNotes: Keep it above 12 °C: cold nights blacken the leaves. Pinch out the flower spikes.
Q38859.funFact: Basil comes from the Greek for royal or kingly plant, perhaps because it was used in royal perfumes. The Latin name was muddled with the basilisk, and basil was once thought to be an antidote to the monster's venom.

Q37083.careNotes: Drought-proof in the ground, but a potted olive still needs regular watering in summer.
Q37083.funFact: The species reaches far beyond the Mediterranean olive: its wild subspecies grow from Madeira and the Canary Islands across Africa and Arabia to south-west China. The 'white' and 'black' olives of South-East Asia are not olives at all but Canarium trees.

Q133754.funFact: The name comes from the Greek for swelling, after the knobbly growth on the flower's fiddle-shaped lip. The genus became so muddled that the American Orchid Society once called it a dumping ground.

Q144412.careNotes: Glochids, its tiny hooked bristles, lodge in the skin: handle it with thick gloves or tongs.
Q144412.funFact: It has long been farmed as a host for cochineal insects, which yield red and purple dyes, a practice dating from before Columbus. In Greek the fruit is called Frankish fig, an old label for foreign produce.

Q310523.careNotes: Glochids, its tiny hooked bristles, lodge in the skin: handle it with thick gloves or tongs.
Q310523.funFact: 'Microdasys' means small and hairy, and instead of spines it carries dense tufts of fine barbed bristles. Those hairs are also shaped to catch fog and channel the water, one reason it does so well in deserts.

Q163196.careNotes: Keep it drier and cooler in winter. It scorches in hot midday sun more than most succulents.
Q163196.funFact: Its star-shaped, maroon-speckled flowers may give off a faint smell of rotting meat to lure the insects that pollinate them. Despite names like starfish cactus, it is not a true cactus.

Q134283.funFact: The name traces back through Spanish and Latin to the Greek origanon, which some read as 'mountain joy', though that origin is disputed. Most of its punchy flavour comes from two compounds, carvacrol and thymol.

Q935848.careNotes: It folds its leaves at night. Now and then it dies back without warning: stop watering, rest it dry for a while, and it resprouts.
Q935848.funFact: Its clover-like leaves, the reason for the name false shamrock, fold down at night. They move not by growing but by changing water pressure in cells at the base of each leaflet.

Q310500.careNotes: Its trunk stores some water, so it takes drier soil than most indoor trees.
Q310500.funFact: Most braided money trees sold in shops are really a close cousin, Pachira glabra, after an early mix-up in Taiwan. The true species is a swamp tree whose huge flowers peel open like a banana to show a shaving brush of stamens.

Q1457960.funFact: Its name means 'thick plant bearing eggs', after the plump, egg-shaped leaves, whose pale blue bloom makes them look like sugared almonds. Wild plants cling to rocky cliffs in San Luis Potosí, Mexico.

Q1278160.careNotes: It drops its leaves in a cool winter: keep it nearly dry and above 12 °C.
Q1278160.funFact: Despite the name Madagascar palm, it is no palm at all but a spiny stem succulent that does much of its photosynthesis through its silvery trunk.

Q938691.funFact: Lutea means yellow, but the yellow is not the flower: it comes from the overlapping bracts. The real flowers are white and short-lived, slipping out from between the bracts one after another.

Q131523.careNotes: It has no water-storing pseudobulbs, so keep the mix evenly moist, never dry. It takes lower light than most orchids.
Q131523.funFact: The name joins Paphos, the Cypriot city sacred to Aphrodite, with the Greek for slipper, yet none grow on Cyprus. Insects trapped in the pouch must climb out past the pollen to escape.

Q143021.funFact: It is named after Wilhelm Lenninghaus, a German who moved to Porto Alegre, Brazil, in the 1880s and collected cacti there. Botanists moved it through four other genera before settling on Parodia.

Q137551.funFact: Its heavily ribbed, spiny ball can spread to 45 cm across while staying under 15 cm tall. Wild plants grow in cool, dry grassland in southern Brazil, and older books list it as Notocactus or Eriocactus.

Q161120.funFact: It is the national flower of Paraguay. Its intricate blooms inspired Christian symbolism, with each part standing for a different piece of the Passion of Christ.

Q156790.careNotes: Tender: it needs frost-free winters and a warm, sunny wall to set fruit.
Q156790.funFact: Around 1700, missionaries in Brazil used the flower to teach the story of the Crucifixion, calling it the flower of the five wounds. That is where the passion in passion fruit comes from.

Q164306.careNotes: Unlike most balcony flowers, it likes to dry out a little between waterings. Overwinter it in a cool, bright, frost-free room, kept nearly dry.
Q164306.funFact: Its genus name comes from the Greek for stork, because the fruit looks like a stork's bill. In Cyprus, where it is called kiouli, it scents syrups and spoon sweets, and in Morocco it goes into mint tea.

Q160925.careNotes: Unlike most balcony flowers, it likes to dry out a little between waterings. Overwinter it in a cool, bright, frost-free room, kept nearly dry.
Q160925.funFact: Peltatum means shield-bearing, because the leaf stalk joins near the centre of the blade, making each leaf shield-like. The governor of the Cape Colony sent it to the Netherlands in 1700.

Q6566235.careNotes: Unlike most balcony flowers, it likes to dry out a little between waterings. Overwinter it in a cool, bright, frost-free room, kept nearly dry.
Q6566235.funFact: Everyone calls it a geranium, but it belongs to Pelargonium, not the genus Geranium. It is a garden hybrid of two wild South African species, one of which was collected at the Cape in 1689 and grown by the Duchess of Beaufort in England.

Q7161522.careNotes: Unlike most ferns, it likes the soil a little drier between waterings, and rots if kept wet.
Q7161522.funFact: Found wild only in New Zealand's scrub and forests, it carries more than 30 pairs of round, leathery leaflets on a single frond. Its name, rotundifolia, simply means round-leaved.

Q7166263.funFact: Its genus is sometimes nicknamed radiator plants, because many peperomias enjoy bright, dry spots such as a windowsill above a radiator.

Q11167712.funFact: The species name, argyreia, means silvery, after the curved silver stripes that make each leaf look like a tiny watermelon. It actually belongs to the pepper family and has nothing to do with watermelons.

Q7166267.funFact: Peperomias are sometimes nicknamed radiator plants, a name perhaps coined by the botanist L. H. Bailey, because many enjoy bright, dry spots like a windowsill above a radiator.

Q11815586.funFact: In the wild it grows only in Jamaica. It takes its common name, red-edge peperomia, from the dark red tinge along the rims of its leaves.

Q15605097.funFact: Its leaves are folded into tubes like green bean pods, with see-through 'windows' along the top. A variety from above 2,000 m has curved leaves like unripe bananas, hence its name musifolia, 'banana leaf'.

Q1328549.funFact: Most peperomia flowers have no noticeable scent, but this one's give off a strong, foul smell likened to mouse urine. The top of each leaf has a V-shaped window that shows the pale green inside.

Q11815596.funFact: Kew Gardens has grown it since 1815. It stands out among peperomias for its thick, heart-shaped leaves covered in soft, felt-like down.

Q7166271.funFact: 'Obtusifolia' means blunt-leaved. It is so easily mixed up with Peperomia magnoliifolia that some botanists once treated them as one species; living plants give it away with their waxier leaves.

Q15606665.funFact: It grows like a tiny tree, its leaf stalks acting as branches that end in glossy, teardrop-shaped leaves, each joined to its stalk in the middle rather than at the edge.

Q22108964.funFact: Peperomias are sometimes called radiator plants, a name perhaps coined by the botanist L.H. Bailey because many enjoy bright, dry spots like a windowsill above a radiator. Their tiny berries dry out to reveal a seed like a grain of pepper.

Q11815594.funFact: In the wild it trails over tree branches, rotten logs and rock cracks in tropical forests, its tiny button-like leaves weaving in and out of one another.

Q11815595.funFact: Its genus, Peperomia, has over 1,000 species, and their small berries dry out to reveal a tiny seed like a peppercorn. Peperomias are sometimes called radiator plants, as many enjoy a bright, dry spot like a sill above a radiator.

Q11815597.funFact: Peperomias are sometimes called radiator plants, a name possibly coined by the botanist L. H. Bailey because so many enjoy bright, dry spots like a windowsill above a radiator.

Q3336567.funFact: Tetraphylla is Greek for four leaves, after the leaves that grow in whorls of three or four. It was first described in 1832 from a coastal survey of South America led by Captain F.W. Beechey.

Q15605793.funFact: Its leaves grow in whorls of five, grey-green above and red underneath. In its Caribbean home it often grows perched on other plants as an epiphyte.

Q37153.careNotes: Grown from a stone, it needs a large pot and a sunny spot. Pinch out the tip to make it branch.
Q37153.funFact: Guacamole comes from the Aztec word ahuacamolli, meaning avocado sauce. People on the coast of Peru were already eating avocados some 10,500 years ago.

Q25284.funFact: The name goes back to the Greek petroselinon, meaning rock celery. Parsley also has a place on the Passover Seder plate, where it stands for the Jews flourishing after they first came to Egypt.

Q160825.funFact: The word petunia comes through French from pétun, a Tupi-Guarani word for tobacco, which belongs to the same nightshade family along with tomatoes and potatoes.

Q133897.careNotes: After flowering, cut the stem just above the second node from the bottom, and it may flower again from there.
Q133897.funFact: Moth orchid is a straight translation: Phalaenopsis means moth-like in Greek. In some wild species the flowers do not wilt after pollination but turn green and fleshy and photosynthesise like leaves.

Q15313108.funFact: It is named after Frieda Billiet, who found it in lowland rainforest in French Guiana; living plants were then grown at Belgium's National Botanic Garden in Meise. It stands out for its orange-yellow leaf stalks.

Q15313128.funFact: Philodendron is Greek for 'tree lover'. Some philodendrons that sprout on the forest floor creep towards the darkest spot nearby, usually a tree's shadow, and only switch to growing towards the light once they reach a trunk.

Q15312979.funFact: In the wild it climbs pressed tight against its host tree in seasonally dry parts of Colombia, Brazil and Bolivia. The heavy silver marbling it is known for appears on its young leaves.

Q4484253.funFact: Erubescens means blushing, a nod to its red stems and deep red, scented spathes. The wild plant is a climber from Colombia, but most of its many hybrid cultivars are self-heading and form compact clumps instead.

Q11071985.careNotes: It crawls along the ground rather than climbing: give it a long, wide pot so its stem can creep across the soil.
Q11071985.funFact: Rather than climbing trees like many philodendrons, it crawls along the forest floor in Colombia, its roots gripping fallen logs, big tree roots and even rocks as the stem creeps forward.

Q15314045.funFact: Its genus name, Philodendron, is Greek for tree-loving. Some philodendrons heat up their flowers to attract the beetles that pollinate them, using oxygen at a rate close to that of a hummingbird.

Q4484257.funFact: Its genus name joins the Greek for love and tree, fitting for a climber that likes to scramble up tree trunks. Because it can grow with roots both in and out of the soil, botanists count it as a semi-epiphyte.

Q2897229.funFact: Melanochrysum means black gold, after tiny golden sparkles on its near-black leaves in sunlight. The Veitch nursery won a first-class certificate for it at an 1886 show in Liverpool.

Q15314692.funFact: Its oak-like leaves change as the plant grows up, getting bigger and adding more side lobes. In the wet forests of South America it climbs, like many philodendrons, and it is a parent of the hybrid Philodendron 'Florida'.

Q7186055.funFact: Its leaf stalks are red and covered in small bristles, giving it a hairy look that sets it apart from other philodendrons. It grows wild in French Guiana, Suriname and northern Brazil.

Q4484251.funFact: Its genus name is Greek for tree-lover. Some philodendrons heat up their flower spikes to lure beetle pollinators, burning oxygen at a rate close to that of hummingbirds.

Q1231082.careNotes: It copes with drier air than most ferns.
Q1231082.funFact: Its name refers to the golden-brown scales that cover its creeping rhizome. In the wild it rarely grows in the ground, preferring rainforest canopies and the dwarf palms of subtropical forests.

Q164113.careNotes: It takes more sun than most indoor palms.
Q164113.funFact: Named after the orchid collector Carl Roebelen, this palm from Yunnan, Laos and northern Vietnam bears tiny edible fruits that look like small, thin-fleshed dates.

Q1026485.funFact: Raised silvery patches on each leaf give it the name aluminium plant. The stamens of its tiny male flowers burst open when the plant is shaken.

Q3023296.funFact: Its genus is so little studied that estimates of how many species it holds run from 250 to 1,000, and about a third of those in regions not yet surveyed may still be undescribed.

Q3388414.funFact: Its best-known form, 'Moon Valley', has deeply cratered leaves said to resemble the surface of the moon. It is a member of the nettle family.

Q7193859.funFact: Its genus name, Pilea, is Latin for felt cap, after the part of the flower that covers the tiny fruit. With hundreds of species, Pilea is the largest genus in the nettle family.

Q646721.funFact: It is one of only six pileas, out of the genus's 600 or more species, that are grown for their looks.

Q311696.careNotes: Let the top half of the soil dry between waterings, and turn the pot often or it leans toward the light.
Q311696.funFact: A Norwegian missionary, Agnar Espegren, carried cuttings home from Yunnan in 1946, and it spread across Scandinavia from hand to hand. Western botanists did not know what it was until the 1980s, hence the name pass-along plant.

Q309550.funFact: Its genus name, Pilosocereus, means hairy cereus, and this blue species has hairy areoles that sprout golden spines. Flowers in the genus usually open at night and may smell strongly of garlic.

Q161663.careNotes: Mexican butterworts, the usual houseplant kind, need no cold rest. In winter they form small, tight rosettes and want drier soil.
Q161663.funFact: The name comes from the Latin pinguis, fat, after the glossy, greasy-looking leaves, as does the common name butterwort. Those leaves are covered in sticky glands that trap and digest small insects.

Q2170121.careNotes: Usually mounted on a board or in a basket: soak the whole root ball when it feels light, and let it dry a little between soaks. Never remove the brown shield fronds at its base.
Q2170121.funFact: Colonies seem to share out jobs: plants higher up channel water down to those below, which soak it up. A 2021 study suggested this could be the first evidence of eusociality in plants.

Q2296184.funFact: Neither Swedish nor an ivy, it comes from southern Africa. A well-known plant of this species sat above the Oval Office mantel through many presidencies, and White House staff often took home cuttings to share.

Q7204480.careNotes: Water only while it grows, from late summer into autumn, and lightly in spring. Never water while a new pair of leaves forms inside the old one: let the old pair shrivel away first.
Q7204480.funFact: It looks like a small cracked stone, which may help it avoid being eaten. A fresh pair of leaves replaces the old pair each year, and its flowers open in the afternoon and shut at sunset.

Q80685380.funFact: In its native New Caledonia it becomes a tree up to 15 m tall, and adult plants grow leaves much broader than the slim, toothed, coppery leaves of young plants.

Q263162.funFact: Its sticky sepals sometimes trap small creatures up to the size of a housefly. Botanists believe living plumbagos look much like the early ancestors of sundews and other carnivorous plants.

Q1097328.careNotes: It drops its leaves in winter: keep it dry and above 10 °C until new leaves appear.
Q1097328.funFact: The name frangipani comes from an Italian noble family, one of whom created a plumeria-scented perfume in the 16th century. Its evening scent lures hawkmoths, yet the flowers give them little or no nectar in return.

Q5903279.funFact: Polyscias means many-shaded, for leaflets that are glossy dark green on top and paler below. In South-east Asia the young leaves are eaten raw with meat, and in Malaysia and Indonesia it is called kuku garuda, Garuda's claws.

Q7226925.funFact: Sometimes called wild coffee, it is not closely related to real coffee plants at all. Left to grow, the shrub can reach over 7 metres, with leaves often edged in white or pale yellow.

Q3024559.funFact: Its cupped, tear-resistant leaves were used as bowls by early Indonesians, and they still turn up as decorative food wrapping in Indonesian cooking today.

Q159547.careNotes: A succulent: it copes with drought and heat, and wants its soil to dry between waterings. Its flowers open only in sun.
Q159547.funFact: Despite names like moss rose, it is no rose but a closer cousin of carnations and cacti. It is also one of the few plants that runs two kinds of photosynthesis, C4 and CAM, in different cells.

Q2481534.funFact: In South Africa's thickets black rhinos and elephants eat it, and people add it to salads and soups. It can switch between two kinds of photosynthesis depending on how dry the season is.

Q42710597.funFact: Many of its relatives were called Chirita until 2011, when botanists moved them into Primulina. The genus, part of the African violet family, grows mostly on the limestone karst hills of southern China and Vietnam.

Q2050113.funFact: Despite being named after Crete, this fern does not actually grow there. It is native across a huge range, though, from the Mediterranean through Africa and Madagascar to tropical Asia and Japan.

Q13188.funFact: Its name comes from the medieval Latin for seeded apple, and in early English it was the apple of Granada. The French word for it, grenade, went on to name the military grenade.

Q203625.funFact: Its fragrant white trumpet flowers open at night and wilt in the morning sun, and its long, warped seed pods explain the name serpent tree. In the mountains of southern China and Taiwan it grows into a tall tree.

Q623263.funFact: In the wild it huddles along riverbanks, lagoons and shallow swamps, damp pockets in the hot, dry south-west of Madagascar, and it can reach 30 metres, far taller than any pot plant.

Q344764.funFact: Unlike many cacti, it flowers from around the base of its stems rather than the top. It is also the type species, the one that defines the whole Rebutia genus.

Q11834848.funFact: Tetrasperma means four-seeded. In 2021 a single variegated plant sold at an online auction in New Zealand for a record NZ$27,100.

Q164097.funFact: Rhapis comes from the Greek for needle and excelsa is Latin for tall, though it is not the tallest of its genus. As it ages, fibrous sheaths fall away to reveal stems that look like bamboo.

Q87584907.funFact: Since it was first described in 1884, botanists have shuffled it through six genera, including Epiphyllum, Schlumbergera and Hatiora. In the wild it grows on trees in the subtropical rainforests of southern Brazil.

Q136525.funFact: It is the only cactus found wild outside the Americas, growing in tropical Africa and Sri Lanka as well. Nobody is sure how it crossed the Atlantic: migrating birds may have carried it, or it may have travelled on trading ships.

Q291080.funFact: Its genus, Rhipsalis, takes its name from the Greek for wickerwork, after its tangled branches. One member, Rhipsalis baccifera, is the only cactus that grows wild outside the Americas, in Africa and Asia.

Q5366359.careNotes: Hardy: keep it outdoors in part shade, and never let it dry out.
Q5366359.funFact: It was the original Tsutsusi, described in Japan in 1712 by Engelbert Kaempfer from its Japanese name, Kirishima-tsutsuji. The Satsuki azaleas are among its many cultivars.

Q5914721.careNotes: Indoor azaleas like it cool (10 to 15 °C) and never dry: dunk the pot in rain water whenever it feels light.
Q5914721.funFact: The species name honours John Sims, the first editor of a botanical magazine. Common in Hong Kong and wild across southern China, Vietnam and Thailand, it is well known in Chinese gardens but fairly rare in the West.

Q344900.careNotes: Cut off faded flowers, and feed it with a rose or tomato feed. Keep the leaves dry to avoid black spot and mildew.
Q344900.funFact: Modern garden roses owe their habit of flowering again and again to cultivated forms of this Chinese species, though wild plants do not repeat. Crossed with Rosa gigantea, it also led to the tea roses.

Q17251288.funFact: Like other ruschias, it has seed capsules that open when wet and close as they dry, with a thin membrane over the seeds so a single shower cannot wash them all away.

Q1111359.funFact: Officinalis refers to the officina, the monastery storeroom where healing herbs were kept, and the grey-green colour called sage is named after its leaves. The Romans called it the holy herb.

Q102240169.funFact: Its old Latin name, ros marinus, means sea dew. In Australia people wear sprigs on ANZAC Day as a sign of remembrance, and it grows wild on the Gallipoli peninsula.

Q161080.funFact: The compact bedding plants seen in parks and shopping centres are a far cry from the wild form, which stands up to 1.3 m tall in the warm, humid mountains of Brazil and is rarely grown.

Q161174.funFact: The flowers hang upside down over an umbrella-shaped style, so a visiting bee must push in past a stigma and leave under a petal, which prevents self-pollination. One species, the parrot pitcher, even traps tadpoles and small fish during floods.

Q1927560.funFact: In one Ontario population nearly a fifth of plants were found holding young eastern newts, trapped in the rainwater pools of its pitchers. It is also the floral emblem of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Q159002.careNotes: Hardy and happy cool: it can also live outdoors in shade.
Q159002.funFact: Neither a begonia nor a geranium, despite its names, it spreads like a strawberry by sending out thread-thin red runners tipped with baby plants. Two of its five white petals are longer than the rest.

Q312047.careNotes: Buds form after cool nights (10 to 15 °C) and long, dark evenings in autumn.
Q312047.funFact: In its home mountains near Rio de Janeiro it flowers around May, which is autumn in Brazil. Truncata means abruptly cut off, after the squared-off tips of its flat stem segments.

Q9334559.funFact: Pictus is Latin for painted, after the silver splashes on its leaves. Climbing a tree or wall, it grips with sticky roots and lays its leaves flat against the surface, a habit known as shingling.

Q9334569.funFact: Its genus name, Scindapsus, appears in the writings of the ancient author Aelian, who used it for an Indian musical instrument played to tame wild elephants.

Q17774329.funFact: Often misspelled 'adolphii', this Mexican cliff-dweller has gone wild as far away as Sicily and the Canary Islands. Its copper-orange leaves develop red or orange edges when they get plenty of sun.

Q15485390.funFact: Its genus, the stonecrops, is so varied that botanists cannot define it by appearance alone and speak of the Sedum problem when trying to sort it out. Some sedums feed the caterpillars of the endangered San Bruno elfin butterfly.

Q2245759.funFact: In the wild it is known only from two ravines in central Veracruz, Mexico, where it hangs from cliffs of igneous rock. Its leaves drop at the slightest touch, and each fallen leaf can root and grow into a new plant.

Q3477641.funFact: Named after the plant collector Edward Palmer, it is a windowsill favourite in Mediterranean towns, where it roots so easily from cuttings that neighbours pass it from one to another.

Q2706112.funFact: Also known as pork and beans, it is thought to be a garden-made hybrid of two other sedums. Its bean-like leaves blush from green to red in summer as a protective response.

Q7447419.careNotes: A spikemoss rather than a true fern: keep it moist at all times, in humid air. A terrarium suits it.
Q7447419.funFact: Despite the nickname peacock fern, it is not a fern but a spikemoss, from an ancient line of plants. Spores found in 6,000-year-old fossils on Pico settled that it is native to the Azores.

Q90600463.careNotes: A climbing cactus: give it a strong post, warmth and full sun to flower and fruit.
Q90600463.funFact: Scented flowers up to 35 cm across open at night, which is why it goes by names like belle of the night and moonflower. The Latin undatus, meaning wavy, describes the rippled edges of its stem ribs.

Q161390.careNotes: Fully hardy: it lives outdoors through winter, even under snow, as long as the soil drains.
Q161390.funFact: The hairs strung across the tips of its leaves look like spider webs, which is where arachnoideum comes from. Wild plants grow in the Alps, Apennines and Carpathians.

Q161724.careNotes: Fully hardy: it lives outdoors through winter, even under snow, as long as the soil drains.
Q161724.funFact: Tectorum means of the roofs: people grew it on rooftops to ward off lightning, and Charlemagne recommended the practice. One of its old English names is welcome-home-husband-though-never-so-drunk.

Q3955278.funFact: Its species name means 'large tongue'. It looks a lot like common ivy and borrows the name, but it belongs to the daisy family, as its yellow daisy-like flowers give away.

Q1556733.careNotes: Usually sold as a bonsai, and it drops leaves at any change: keep it in one bright, cool spot, evenly moist.
Q1556733.funFact: Bruise a leaf and it gives off a nasty smell, which earned it the old name foetida. Even so, it is one of the most common bonsai sold in Europe and America, also known as tree of a thousand stars.

Q163267.careNotes: It grows from a tuber and rests after flowering: stop watering once the leaves yellow, keep it dry and cool, and repot it when new shoots show.
Q163267.funFact: Its genus honours Wilhelm Sinning, a gardener at the Bonn university botanic garden. It is still sold as gloxinia, a leftover from its first name, though true gloxinias grow from scaly rhizomes rather than tubers.

Q23501.careNotes: Water deeply and evenly: a dry spell followed by a soaking splits the fruit and causes dark, sunken patches at the bottom (blossom end rot). Tie it to a cane as it grows.
Q23501.funFact: Its species name, lycopersicum or 'wolf peach', was borrowed from Galen for a plant nobody has identified, after a 16th-century guess that could not be right. In Italy the fruit was first called pomi d'oro, golden apples.

Q1475749.careNotes: It keeps its berries longer in a cool, bright room (10 to 15 °C).
Q1475749.funFact: Despite its name, it comes from Peru and Ecuador. In Lucy Maud Montgomery's 1935 novel Mistress Pat, one is given as a Christmas present and blamed for a run of bad luck.

Q997566.careNotes: It shrivels fast when dry: keep the soil moist at all times.
Q997566.funFact: Few plants collect as many nicknames, from mind-your-own-business and Paddy's wig to Corsican curse. It is named after Henri-Augustin Soleirol, a French army engineer and amateur botanist who first gathered it on Corsica.

Q761494.careNotes: It droops dramatically when dry and perks up within hours of watering. It flowers in lower light than most aroids, but not in deep shade.
Q761494.funFact: The genus name means spathe-leaf, after the white bract around the flower spike. The species honours Gustav Wallis, a German plant collector, and was found growing wild in Colombia.

Q287520.careNotes: Keep it drier and cooler in winter. It scorches in hot midday sun more than most succulents.
Q287520.funFact: Its star-shaped flowers can be 40 cm across and smell of rotting meat. The stench, along with their size and colour, fools the flies that pollinate them into treating the flower like a carcass.

Q149601.careNotes: It wants more sun than most indoor trees: a south or west window. Its big leaves split in draughts, which is harmless.
Q149601.funFact: It is one of the few plants proven to contain bilirubin, a pigment usually found in animals. Its huge flowers, with white sepals and a bluish-purple 'tongue' above a dark blue bract, can be 45 cm long.

Q148904.careNotes: It wants more sun than most indoor trees: a south or west window. It flowers only once mature and a little pot-bound.
Q148904.funFact: The name reginae honours Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. Its beak-like sheath makes a sturdy perch for sunbirds, and when one lands to drink, a petal opens and dusts its feet with pollen.

Q159180.funFact: Streptocarpus is Greek for twisted fruit, after the spiralling seed pods that look like a narwhal's tusk. DNA studies show that African violets evolved from within this very genus.

Q50870323.funFact: African violets belong to Streptocarpus, a genus named from the Greek for twisted fruit. DNA shows they evolved from within it in Tanzania, even though their own seed pods are not twisted.

Q55212864.funFact: Its genus, Strobilanthes, is famous for species that bloom on long cycles of several years; one of them, Strobilanthes wightii, flowers only once every thirteen years.

Q15338244.funFact: Its synonym, sanguinea, is Latin for blood-red. In its native Brazilian rainforest, hummingbirds and bees do most of the pollinating.

Q15315495.funFact: Like other syngoniums, its flower spike heats itself to about 12°C above the surrounding air and gives off a sharp scent, drawing in the beetles that pollinate it.

Q13403357.funFact: Podophyllum means with foot-like leaves. It was first mistaken for Nephthytis, an African genus, and is still sold under that name even though it comes from Latin America.

Q15246904.funFact: Like other syngoniums, it changes leaf shape as it matures: the simple leaves of young potted plants give way to much more lobed ones on adult vines, which can climb 10 to 20 m up rainforest trees.

Q759876.funFact: Its Nahuatl name means twenty flower, twenty being the base of Aztec counting. The dried petals are even ground into chicken feed to give egg yolks a deeper yellow.

Q99929671.funFact: Its flowers heat themselves by burning fat, holding about 34 °C and sometimes more, which spreads their scent further and lures the beetles that pollinate them.

Q89256996.funFact: It was sold as a chance seedling that appeared in a Western Australian nursery in 1983, and later as plant of the year in 1988. Since then, credible claims say it actually grew from seed collected from a wild plant in Brazil.

Q148668.funFact: Vulgaris means common in the sense of widespread. Thyme tastes a little spicier than oregano and a little sweeter than sage, and it grows wild from the western Mediterranean to southern Italy.

Q157270.funFact: Linnaeus named the genus after the Swedish physician Elias Tillandz. Needing no soil, these plants drink through tiny scales on their leaves and will cling to almost anything, even telephone wires.

Q6824094.funFact: Air plants need no soil: tiny scales on their leaves soak up water from rain and fog. Dry plants look silvery white, and they turn green again as soon as they are wet.

Q7802469.funFact: Its genus is named after Elias Tillandz, a Swedish physician and botanist. Tillandsias take in water through special cells on their leaves, and their seeds drift off on silky parachutes like a dandelion's.

Q1937140.funFact: Ionantha means 'with violet flowers'. Linnaeus named the genus in 1738 after Elias Tillandz, a 17th-century doctor and botanist whose family name was originally Tillander.

Q311524.careNotes: Mist it rather than soak it, then let it dry: hang it where the air moves.
Q311524.funFact: Neither Spanish nor a moss, it is a rootless bromeliad that takes water and nutrients from the air and rain. In Hawaii it was nicknamed after the beard of Sanford B. Dole, and car seats in the early 1900s were padded with it.

Q7802776.careNotes: A silver, fuzzy kind: it takes more sun and less water than green ones. Dunk it briefly rather than soaking it.
Q7802776.funFact: Xerographica comes from Greek words for dry and writing. It perches on the highest branches in dry forests and thorn scrub of Central America, soaking up intense light, and its red to purple flowers are unusually long-lasting.

Q1207043.funFact: Another of its names, trader's compass, comes from an old Uzbek saying that it would point traders the right way, as long as they were of good character. Its scented flowers are distilled into a prized perfume oil.

Q601079.funFact: The genus honours John Tradescant and his son, English naturalists and explorers, while fluminensis refers to people from Rio de Janeiro. Its fleshy stems snap easily, and a piece can root wherever it lands on damp soil.

Q1563504.funFact: Oddly for such a vivid plant, its name pallida means pale, after the washed-out grey-green look of wild specimens. The purple garden form is a cultivar, and its small three-petalled flowers open only in the morning.

Q4461763.funFact: A dense coat of white hairs covers even its buds, shielding it from strong sun and cutting water loss in the dry hills of Nuevo León, Mexico. It is one of the most succulent tradescantias.

Q967979.funFact: Its tiny white flowers sit inside boat-shaped purple bracts, like the infant Moses in his basket among the bulrushes, hence Moses-in-the-cradle. It also goes by oyster plant and boatlily.

Q169381.funFact: The leaves carry two silver stripes on top and deep magenta underneath, but after long spells of strong sun the stripes fade and the whole leaf turns purple. Botanists once gave it a genus of its own, as Zebrina pendula.

Q156288.careNotes: It flowers best in poor soil: skip the feeding, or you get leaves instead of flowers.
Q156288.funFact: Linnaeus's daughter Elisabeth noticed at 19 that the orange flowers seem to flash at dusk, an effect now thought to be a trick of the human eye. The genus name, Tropaeolum, means little trophy.

Q163060.careNotes: A spring bulb: pot it in autumn and keep it cold (below 10 °C) and lightly moist while the roots form, then bring it into the light when shoots appear.
Q163060.funFact: It fuelled Dutch tulip mania in the 1630s, when a single Semper Augustus bulb sold for 6,000 florins in Haarlem, at a time when one florin bought a bushel of wheat. Virus-streaked blooms were the most prized.

Q286061.careNotes: Usually grown bare-root in a basket or vase: soak the roots until they turn green, and give it bright light with some sun.
Q286061.funFact: The name comes from the Sanskrit name for one of its species. Its best-known member, Vanda coerulea, has blue flowers, a colour that is very unusual in the plant world.

Q64683022.funFact: Cyanea means blue, after the intense violet flowers that emerge from its flat pink quill of bracts. DNA studies moved it out of Tillandsia and into Wallisia.

Q15507520.careNotes: It likes drier soil and more sun than most indoor trees: a south window, watered once the soil is dry most of the way down.
Q15507520.funFact: Its flower, the izote, is El Salvador's national flower and a common ingredient in Salvadoran cooking. The swollen base of the trunk, like an elephant's foot, suits its long-used garden name, elephantipes.

Q924592.careNotes: A cycad, not a palm. It wants bright light with some sun, and dry soil between waterings.
Q924592.funFact: Despite the name cardboard palm, it is not a palm but a cycad, with male and female cones on separate plants. Its pollinator is a small cycad weevil.

Q15312475.funFact: The name blends Zamia, a cycad with similar leaves, and culcas, an old Middle Eastern word for its relative taro. Dutch nurseries only began growing it on a large scale around 1996.

Q1945905.careNotes: Keep it moist, even wet, while it's in leaf: in the wild it grows in marshes. It stays evergreen if it never dries out.
Q1945905.funFact: Since 1926 it has been a symbol of Irish republicanism, used to remember those who died in the Easter Rising of 1916. It was also the national flower of Saint Helena, where it grows so freely that it counts as an invasive weed.

Q3240203.careNotes: It flowers after a good soak that follows a dry spell, hence the name rain lily.
Q3240203.funFact: Its genus name joins Zephyrus, the Greek god of the west wind, with the Greek for flower. Rain lilies earned their other name by bursting into bloom shortly after a rainstorm, sometimes all at once in what breeders call a blitz.

Q15245321.funFact: Wild plants in Mexico stand barely ankle-high, yet the garden zinnias bred from them include giants with flower heads up to 15 cm across. The genus honours the German botanist Johann Gottfried Zinn.

Q133749.funFact: The name comes from the Greek for yoke, after the yoke-like growth at the base of the lip. It is also the only orchid genus whose abbreviation is just the letter Z.
